House proceeded to further consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Mclsaac, that the House go into committee on Bill (No. 103) relating to an agreement between the government of Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway Company respecting certain railways.

Mr. Speaker, at the last session of the House, when this order of business expired, I was speaking to an amendment to the motion now on the Order paper, as follows :
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted therefor : ' It is the opinion of this House that the Bill be not passed until the subject of the proposed legislation has been submitted by direct reference to the electors of Manitoba in order that their wish in respect to the same may be ascertained.'
I went briefly over the history of what is now known as the Manitoba deal, outlining the liabilities wbicb the province bad assumed and the risks it ran, and the position of tbe Canadian Northern Railway Company in reference to this deal. I did so because 1 wanted to give tbe House some information regarding tbe public sentiment In the province of Manitoba in respect to this Bill.
I did so also because during the time the matter was pending before tlie local legislature, tbe provincial premier and tbe members of tbe local government promised time and again to all parties that all other matters should be dealt with and provided for before tbe contracts went through the legislature ; and they kept on telling them so until as a matter of fact tbe contracts wrent through the legislature without any vital amendments being made. I propose, without trespassing on tbe time of tbe House any more than is necessary, to give some information regarding public sentiment on this question in tlie city of Winnipeg and tlie province of Manitoba, because the motion which I put on the paper is rather a novel one. At tlie same time, looking at the Bills as they stand to-day, it seems to me that the most feasible and sensible plan that can possibly be proposed is that before this parliament gives these Bills its sanction. the contracts shall be referred to the people of Manitoba themselves by a direct reference, in order that they may express their opinion either for or against them.

I think that is necessary, because the proposition is a gigantic one for so small a province. Nothing that has been done there hitherto can have the influence on the future of that province that this bargain will have. I am going to refer in the first place to the representations and resolutions of public bodies in Winnipeg. I may say that I have never known such unanimity of opinion in the city of Winnipeg on any question as there is in opposition to these contracts. To prove that, I am going to refer to the action of the city council itself, to public meetings that have been held in the city, to the action of the Board of Trade, the Trade and Labour Council and the Labour party of Winnipeg, and to the business publication, the Winnipeg Commercial. All these agree in asking that more time be allowed to the people of the province to consider the proposition contained in these contracts. The city council is not in the habit of taking up matters that are before the local legislature ; but it was practically forced to take up this matter, because in the near future it expects to offer for sale about $750,000 worth of bonds. Just a week after these contracts were put through the Manitoba legislature, the municipality of Westbourne offered its bonds to the First National Bank of Chicago, one of the largest handlers of such securities on this continent; but the bank replied to the agent who offered the bonds, that it did not care even to make an offer for them on account of the province proposing to involve itself in such tremendous liabilities. The controller of the city of Winnipeg gave it as his opinion to the Finance Committee that if these Bills became law, they would seriously interfere with the sale of the city's bonds and would have a very serious effect on their price ; and the Finance Committee asked the city council to pass a resolution, which I will read to the House :
Your committee have considered the proposed agreement between the provincial government and the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They feel that the action of the government in taking the people into their confidence is worthy of all praise, and could only have been done with a view, not of making useless discussion, but of profiting from suggestions that might be made.
It will have been observed that many prominent citizens who have approved of the deal, have only done so on the assumption that the interests of the province have been safeguarded at all points, while the adverse comments of our shrewdest business men, irrespective of party, who have carefully gone into the matter, make it apparent that the consensus of opinion is that the liabilities to be assumed are too great for the resources of the province.
It is not necessary here to recapitulate the many objectionable features' of the agreement, as they have already been gone into, suffice it to say that the main features are excessive capitalization of the Northern Pacific lines, too great a bonded guarantee,. a liability of $600,000 per annum, with no recourse against the
company in case of default, and apparently no penalty clauses.
It is almost certain that as soon as the new road is in a position to compete for freight, the Canadian Pacific Railway would, in selfdefence, initiate a rate war, which would mean that the province would have immediately to meet the fixed charges, with but one result-
' ruin '!
Therefore, in the interests of the city of Winnipeg, whose welfare is inseparable from that of the province, we would strongly and respectfully urge the government to either withdraw the present agreement or to so amend it as to meet the vital objections that have been urged against it.
This resolution was carried in the city council of Winnipeg, and it expresses what is practically the sentiment of all the opposition that has been brought against these Bills. The Winnipeg Board of Trade, which is a very large body, took, of course, a great interest'in this contract. They held special meetings and invited the premier of the province to address these meetings, which he did. They appointed some committees to consider ail the matters involved and to make suggestions to the local government, which suggestions the local government had invited, and then, finding that they really could get no satisfaction, they passed this resolution :
Resolved, that this board disapproves of the contracts and acts affecting the Northern Paclflc Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, as drawn and brought before the legislature. And, in view of the great importance of the subject, the great liability to be assumed by the province, the number of railway proposals recently made to the government and the uncertainty as to future railway extension, this board is of opinion that the Acts confirming the contracts should not be passed at this session of the legislature, but that ample time should be given the country to study fully the whole railway situation.
It was then common knowledge that several propositions had been made to the Manitoba government of a similar nature to the one finally accepted, and the board of trade considered that the people had not had sufficient time to thoroughly look into the various proposals. But, after the fullest consideration that could be given the whole matter, it became evident that the government had not made a wise selection, and that the proposition they had accepted was given the preference, for some reason or other, without regard to the resources of the province and the obligations incurred. The hoard of trade, therefore, asked that the matter should be suspended until the consensus of opinion of the people was obtained. They considered that, in a matter so vitally concerning everybody in the province, the local legislature had not shown fairness or discretion of a legitimate regard for the opinion of the people, in taking up this railway proposition and hurrying it through all its stages, and then presenting it to the Dominion parliament at the very

last moment, and attempting to hurry it through that body. It is not often that you find all the public bodies and organizations of a large city agreeing on a matter of this kind, in which, necessarily, party politics must be to a considerable extent involved, as these bodies have agreed together in the city of Winnipeg. The next resolution was one passed unanimously by the Labour party of that city. They condemned the contract as hasty and unwise. They stated :
That the Winnipeg labour party, after two weeks' further consideration of the railway proposals of the provincial government, finds no reason to recede from the position taken by the party at a meeting on February 20th, when a resolution condemning the scheme was passed. That having examined the explanations offered by the government, both inside and outside the House, such examination leaves our objections substantially as before.
And whereas, we believing as we do that ownership is essential to any real control, finding this principle, both for the present and future, eliminated from the contracts except under the most onerous conditions, which secure every advantage and all increment in value to the Canadian Northern, we believe it would be an abandonment of our principles if we failed In offering our strenuous opposition to the proposals.
We are further confirmed in our distrust of the government by the indecent and unnecessary haste with which a matter of such magnitude has been hurried through every stage in the legislature, and hereby pledge ourselves to use our utmost endeavours to secure disallowance, by appealing to the Lieutenant Governor to withhold his assent until such time as the will of the people has been ascertained beyond doubt, and failing that, to endeavour to secure disallowance by the Dominion parliament.
And ns late as last week, this same body passed a further resolution sustaining its previous action :
Whereas, in the opinion of this party, public sentiment in Manitoba, irrespective of party politics, is decidedly averse to the ratification of the Manitoba government's contracts with the Northern Pacific and Canadian Northern railways. And whereas, repeated appeals from representative bodies of all classes of citizens and parties to have the matter submitted to the people have been ineffectual; be it resolved, that we appeal to the Dominion parliament to withhold its sanction to the contracts until they have been endorsed by the electorate of the province.
The Trade and Labour Council of the city took up the matter at an early stage- and this body I consider one of the most important in Winnipeg, for it is made up of delegates from other bodies, representing practically all the organized mechanics in the city. This body dealt specially with the contract, in view of the argument made in its favour, both in Ottawa and Winnipeg, that it involved the principle of government ownership, which was one of the planks in the platform of the party now in power in Manitoba during the last election. But that plea, of course, has not met with any Mr. PUTTEE.
credence in the city of Winnipeg, although I have been asked several times why I should oppose this measure, seeing that 1 am in favour of the government ownership and operation of railways. The Winnipeg Trade and Labour Council dealt with the question as follows :
Whereas, section No. 6 of the platform of principle? adopted by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and concurred in by this council, is as follows :-
' Public ownership of all franchises, such as railways,' &c.
And whereas, by an Act of the provincial legislature of Manitoba it is proposed to offer inducements to a private corporation to build and operate further railways in Manitoba, such inducements being in the form of the guaranteeing of interest and other pecuniary obligations of a very extensive character.
And whereas, such Act or Acts of the legislature of Manitoba dees not provide for or recognize the principle of government ownership ;
And whereas, the declared principle of this council is as set forth in the said 6th section of the platform of principles adopted by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada;
Therefore, be it resolved that this council petition the member for Winnipeg to oppose to his utmost extent the measure now before the parliament of Canada, which proposes to confirm the Acts of the Manitoba legislature which have reference to agreements between the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
Then follows a list of the members of parliament to whom they sent this resolution.
But one of the most striking expressions of opinion that was ever given in the city, was given by an immense mass meeting at which there were present the three members of the local legislature. When speaking of public opinion in Winnipeg, I think it well to point out that for the provincial elections, the city is divided into three divisions, and that each division returned at the last election a supporter of the present Manitoba government. But, notwithstanding that fact, and notwithstanding the fact that these three members were present, this large meeting passed the following resolution, on a vote of five to one :
Whereas, at a mass meeting of the citizens of the city of Winnipeg, held in Selkirk hall on Saturday, the 23rd day of February last, a resolution was almost unanimously passed protesting against the carrying out of the proposed contracts between the government of Manitoba and the Northern Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company;
And whereas, the said contracts have also been condemned by the board of trade of Winnipeg by a vote of 36 to 12, and also by mass meetings held at various points in the province and also by the city council of the city of Winnipeg ;
And whereas, in spite of such protests and without sufficient change, the said contracts have been ratified by the legislature of Manitoba ;
And whereas, in order to carry Into effect the provisions of the said contract, It is necessary

that confirmatory legislation be obtained from the parliament of Canada ;
And whereas, an application is being made to the parliament of Canada for such legislation as aforesaid ;
And whereas, it is the opinion of this mass meeting assembled in the Winnipeg theatre this 15th day of March, that the said contracts are not in the interests of the province of Manitoba, inasmuch as the said contracts do not secure the building of any new additional railroads, and there is no positive assurance that they will bring about any reduction of rates, and inasmuch as they involve the province of Manitoba in a liability which, if called upon to pay, would seriously embarrass the financial position of the province; and that the contracts should not be ratified unless and until the electors of the province of Manitoba have had an opportunity of signifying their wishes at the polls with reference to the same ;
It is therefore resolved :
1.	That the Dominion government and the Dominion parliament be memorialized, asking them .to refuse to pass the proposed legislation ratifying the said contracts until the people of Manitoba have pronounced upon the said contracts as aforesaid ;
2.	It is recommended that delegations he sent to Ottawa to urge upon the Dominion parliament to accede to the wishes of the people of Manitoba, and to withhold their consent to the said bargains as aforesaid.
And there are further sections dealing with the delegation. The outcome of this meeting was the appointment of a citizens' committee, a large and representative committee, to keep track of the progress of this Bill, both in the province and at Ottawa. And I have here a telegram that was read before the Railway Committee, which I wish to have put along with the other evidence of the public opinion in the city of Winnipeg :
Winnipeg, Man., April 27th.
The following resolution was passed unanimously at a meeting of the citizens committee held to-day. ' Whereas the Canadian Northern mn-tract-was passed By the legislature on the strength of the premier's statements in and out of the House that the province, would have absolute control of rates and that if the province had not such control that the contract was bad and would not be passed. And whereas the Attorney General stated that all defects would be remedied in the mortgage and inserted a clause in the Act for that purpose which clause the railway company state to be useless and it is to be struck out and whereas an amendment is now proposed under which it is made clear that the province cannot control the rates and whereas such an amendment does away with the whole basis of the contract and leaves the province liable on a guarantee which they could not meet except by direct taxation, and a contract such as it would then be, has never been approved of or voted on either by the legislature or the people and would undoubtedly be rejected almost unanimously by the people if submitted to them and whereas the feeling in the city and the province so far as heard from with reference to the proposed amendments is unanimously against them, as there is nothing left of the contract but the liability of the province which will and
must end disastrously both for the province and Dominion. Therefore be it resolved that this citizens committee demand that the matter be referred hack to the legislature to be reconsidered by them.'
This, it will be observed was of very recent date-April 27th. The committee states that the people of Manitoba are almost unanimously opposed to these deals. I do not know that I would care to make any such broad assertion, but there is such widespread opposition as to make my plea at all events one of common sense, that an opportunity should be given to the people on direct reference irrespective of all other issues and parties, to say whether they are or are not favourable to these contracts. I think the evidence I have given makes it pretty clear that the opinion of the city of Winnipeg is decidedly against this contract. The city of Winnipeg is by no means all of Manitoba. It is from one-fifth to-one-sixth of the province in population. It is entitled also to this further consideration- that it is the seat of government, and is where the daily papers are published, and its people are thus in a better position to give due and speedy consideration to matters of this kind. These Acts were passed through the local legislature before the people in the rural districts had had an opportunity to thoroughly consider them. In a sparsely settled country like that, the people must depend for their general information upon the weekly issues of the daily papers, and ofttimes such news is eight or nine days old before it reaches the people. It must be remembered also that when these contracts w-ere first published the newspapers themselves bad not had time to consider them and give any decided opinion upon them. The press in Winnipeg and in Manitoba generally dealt with these contracts most fairly, and neither condemned nor approved them for partisan reasons

The
newspapers put the contracts before the people and reserved, If not comment, at least approval or condemnation, until such time as the contracts had been thoroughly looked into. But all this takes time, and so the people in the rural districts were not able to give an opinion In anything like as quick a time as the people of Winnipeg. I have here a batch of resolutions passed by public meetings and municipal councils, and forwarded to the delegates at Ottawa. I think that these are entitled to as much, if not more, consideration than are the expressions of opinion of the people of Winnipeg, because bon. members will understand that in a country like that, when a railway deal of any kind is proposed, and the promoters make offers and promises to the people which awake expectations of branch lines, railway shops, bridges, improvements or works of one kind or another, these things ai-e a great inducement, and people are apt not to look into the broad merits I of the proposition, but to look at its prospec-

tive value In the profit it may yield to their particular section. Some of the resolutions here are of identical wording, but X will only read the first one of these, and also others that weke drafted at the meetings at which they were passed, and which generally refer to some particular point. A note says that this was carried by a large majority I have one from the town of Selkirk, one of the most important towns in the province, about 24 miles north-east of Winnipeg, and it is noted as being carried unanimously. I have also one from the Icelandic citizens of the town of Selkirk. The Icelanders in Selkirk constitute a very large proportion of the population. The meeting at which these resolutions were passed were held in separate halls, but they were hold upon the same date. I do not wish to refer more than is necessary to newspaper comment, but, as I have stated before, all the newspapers most certainly treated these contracts very fairly when they were first published, and their position since then has been determined by the merits or demerits, as they have been discovered, in the contracts themselves. But, business knows no politics, and I wish to quote from the principal business publication of the west, the Winnipeg Commercial. No man who comes from the west or who knows this paper will charge it for one minute with having its opinions influenced in matters of this kind by political considerations. On March 2. the Winnipeg Commercial contained the following ;
The all-absorbing question in Manitoba is now the railway contract entered into between the provincial government and the Northern Pacific and the Canadian Northern Railway Companies. While much attention is being given to this matter throughout all Canada, here the most | intense interest is being taken in the question.

The first effect of the announcement made by Premier Roblin of the contract entered into with the railway companies was one of surprise. The boldness of the proposals and the enormous financial obligations which would be imposed upon the province by the final ratification of the contract were such as to bewilder thinking persons, who took the trouble to study out what the contract really meant. As soon as sufficient time had developed to permit of the careful study of the agreement, it became evident that there would be a very strong opposition to the acceptance of the proposals by the legislature. This opposition has developed rapidly, and is evidently gaining in strength from day to day, as the document is discussed and gone into by the people.
At a later part of the article the obligation that the province assumes under these contracts is noted :
The obligation assumed by the province we may briefly sum up as follows :-Northern Pacific lines, $7,000,000, or equivalent to the annual interest in that sum at, say, 4 per cent. Guarantee of the bonds of the Ontario and Rainy River section for 200 miles at $20,000 per mile, equal to $5,800,000. The annual interest charge will amount to $232,000 on the Rainy River section and the Northern Pacific rental, first ten years, will amount to $210,000 per year, or a total of $442,000 annual interest charge, which the province will be liable for. In addition to this, we have the liability of the province in connection with previous guarantees of bonds covering sections of the Canadian Northern system in Manitoba, which would bring the total annual liability of the provice for interest charges and rental of the Northern Pacific lines up to about $000,000, or a sum nearly equal to the total annual revenue of the province.
It must be seen from this statement of facts that the final ratification of these contracts will leave the province in a thoroughly impoverished condition financially for many years to come, so that no matter what favourable opportunities may arise in the future, the province will be effectually barred from taking advantage of them while this load of responsibility is hanging over us. It would probably make it impossible for the province to float bonds on a profitable basis for years, no matter how urgent may be the necessity for such action. It is also possible that our municipal securities would be adversely affected for a time. Of course, as the road became an established and paying enterprise this difficulty would be overcome ; but with almost a certainty that the province would be called upon to make good annual deficits during the first few years of the operation of the road, it is quite sure that our credit would be mo3t seriously affected in the world's money markets.
While there are many more important points which might be referred to, including several serious objections on other grounds which might be urged against the contract, these will not be touched upon at present. What is most urgent now' is time to thoroughly go into the matter. The country should have months to discuss and digest the contracts, and this should be done in a fair, independent and non-partisan spirit. We believe there is a disposition among the people to consider this matter as much as possible independent of party politics. In a question of such vital importance to the future of this province, we cannot afford to look at the matter through party spectacles. Premier Rob-Mr. PUTTEE.
iin has himself shown a disposition to take the people into his confidence, and he has asked for and declared that he is, ' wide open ' to receive suggestions and information upon the question. We believe he is honest in his opinions upon the question, and we furthermore believe he will gain the almost universal respect of the people of Manitoba by giving ample time to allow of the thorough discussion and crystallization of public opinion upon the most momentous matter which has yet come before the people of Manitoba. No harm can result from allowing the matter to stand even if it should go over to another session of the legislature. It is not a case in which delays will be dangerous, while to hurry the matter through would be an indication of weakness on the part of the government, and also an evidence of weakness in the contract itself.
The remarkable thing to me is, that, with all this advice, well meant and well directed, the government should have insisted and finally did insist on putting these measures through the local House without removing the very vital objections that were pointed out. I consider that the Winnipeg Commercial and the others from which I have quoted were justified in asking for time for a proper investigation and for proper consideration on behalf of the province. The strange thing is that the local government all the while promised that such consideration should be given, and that yet, in spite of the request on the one side and the granting of it on the other, they went ahead and put the Bills through the legislature just as rapidly as they possibly could do it Now, I have asked in my resolution that these Bills should not be allowed to become law until they have been referred by a direct reference to the people of Manitoba. I think this is as good a suggestion as we can get, because I believe that in all these matters the people themselves should have the final determination. The Bills that passed the Manitoba legislature are not ordinary legislative Acts. They are not Acts that can be amended next year, that can be revised, or that can be tampered with by any other government. Neither are they Acts that can be repealed by any other government. If the government allows this Bill to pass and the guarantee of Manitoba is at the back of these bonds, then, there is no such thing ns tampering with the legislation afterwards, and the whole thing would be done in spite of the protests of the people of the country. The future of the province w'ould be mortgaged to a tremendous extent without listening either in the legislature or in this House to the request of the people for an opportunity to express their voice on this question.
Would the hon. gentleman tell the House, if a referendum has been taken on such questions in this country, or in Switzerland, or in other European countries.

When I put this motion on the paper I thought it well to do so in

order that the opinion of the people might be obtained. In ease the Bill should go into committee, I have given notice of motion that it shall not become law until such time as it has been passed upon by the people of the province. At that stage,
I intend to deal with the question of the referendum, which is one of great interest to me.
Would the hon. gentleman not think that the fact that a plebiscite was taken on the temperance question in Canada, would form a proper precedent for the taking of a plebiscite now.

I do not know that it would have anything to do with this question. Personally, I am favourable to the recognition of the principle of the referendum under our system. I have been told by one of the members of this parliament that I did not understand the constitution I was living under; that there was no such thing as a referendum arranged for under our parliamentary system. But I think that gentleman has given too much importance to what he thinks are the limita-' tions of this parliament. We have a perfect right to make a condition in passing a Bill that it must get the ratification of the people, or any other ratification before it becomes law. I have a few other points, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to refer too, but it is now six o'clock.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

It has not been my in-* tention, in speaking to this motion, to go into the merits of the Bill, but simply to show the state of the public mind with regard to it. I have given evidence of that this afternoon. So far as Manitoba is concerned this is not merely a legislative Act; it is not an Act that can be amended next session; it is not an Act that the next government can repeal or amend; but after it is made valid by this parliament, the Bill becomes a contract and the guarantee of Manitoba goes behind $17,000,000 worth of bonds, and for thirty years at least there is no reopening of the question. That is such a long time in the light of railway development in the west, that it is practically pledging the province for all time. Therefore, some extraordinary course is necessary. It is quite plain that if it were the law and custom in Manitoba to submit important matters like this to the referendum, such an Act would never have been passed. The legislature would not think of passing a law that it knew the people would not assent to. As a matter of fact the legislature should not do so. If such Bills as this were to go to the people before they became law, we never would have such pro-140
positions before our legislative bodies. This lias been the experience in places where they have the referendum. In North Dakota where they have had the referendum *incorporated in their law for some years, it has never been availed of. When we were discussing this matter in the west, we took the trouble to find out whether this was because of a defect in the Dakota referendum law, or whether it was placed on the statute books without any intention of enforcing it. The governor of North Dakota set the matter at rest by replying : Since this referendum law has been a part of our constitution we have had no charter-mongers, no railway speculators, no wildcat schemes submitted to our legislature. Formerly our time was occupied by speculative schemes of one kind or another, but since the referendum has been made part of the constitution, these people do not press their schemes on the legislature, and hence there is no necessity for having recourse to the referendum. I would also call attention to the fact that the province of Manitoba has no second Chamber, and that when an Act has passed the legislative assembly it becomes law if it receives the assent of the Governor in Council. Under our system of government we recognize the necessity of some kind of a check or revising power over any one House. I do not think myself that we have the best system that could be procured in that way. I do not think, for instance, that an appointive assembly should revise the work of an elective assembly. But, the fact of our having two Houses here, and some of the provinces having them, is a recognition of the principle, that a single House is not always to be trusted in matters of legislation. I would in all cases substitute the referendum for a second Chamber. I think it would be better, safer and more satisfactory if all our important legislation were necessarily submitted to a referendum vote of the people, who elect this body. TVe are here only as representatives ; our only business is to endeavour to carry out the will of the people who send us here. I do not believe there would be the least harm in having the present Bill referred strictly to a referendum vote of the people in whose name it is being enacted, namely, the people of Manitoba. I propose that because it seems to me altogether a preferable manner of ascertaining the real sentiment of the people to what an ordinary political general election is. Even if an election were held on this question, it would not be carried simply on the merits of the question itself, but ail the usual party considerations would creep in. The only way to get a proper expression of the people upon any one measure Is to submit that measure by itself for a direct answer, yes or no. as to whether it shall become law. Then, delay is a very important factor at the present time in this matter, because, as I have pointed out,



when these Bills were before the .Manitoba legislature, to every suggestion that was made, or every amendment that was proposed, the public were told that everything, would be provided for in the mortgage. It appears to me that even we in this House should go no further with this Bill until we have all the measure before us. There is to be a mortgage, which is to include a great deal more than the Act of the legislature includes. We are now dealing with a measure which is only half a measure ; we are dealing with a matter in regard to which we have not all the essential papers or documents. In the Railway Committee it was asked that before we proceeded any further the mortgage provided for in the Bill should be laid on the Table. It seems to me that is a more important part of the matter than the Bill which we have before us ; and if the measure were laid over until such time as a referendum vote could be had in the province of Manitoba, the mortgage could be prepared, and all the facts got before the people. With these explanations, I move my amendment.

Mr. Speaker, before the amendment is adopted, I wish to make a few remarks. I myself gave notice of a resolution to the effect that the Bill should not be passed until it was referred back to the legislature of Manitoba, because the Bill which this House has been asked to ratify is not the Bill that was passed by the local legislature. In fact, there are such important differences that I think it would be unwise, unpatriotic, and unfair of this House to force upon the people of Manitoba a contract which was not ratified, and would not be ratified by the legislature, and which must be wholly repugnant to at least three-fourths of the people of Manitoba. I do not want to speak at too great a length on this question ; but, I doubt if a more important issue has ever come before the Dominion of Canada. I doubt whether any more important question has ever been dealt with by this House ; and that statement should be a sufficient warrant to you, Sir, and to the members of this House, to demand that the fullest and most complete investigation of everything connected with it should be made before this House ratifies this great wrong, which by that ratification, must necessarily be inflicted upon the people of Manitoba. I regret very much that the House is not more full to-night, in order that the arguments which I may advance, however feebly, might be heard; because, although considerable discussion on this Bill occurred in the Railway Committee. still I am quite satisfied that a vast number of the members of this House know nothing about its provisions, and are not in a position to cast an intelligent vote on the question. In addition to that, since I came to Ottawa I have found, in my intercourse with members of this House, that the
view seems to be generally taken that they have nothing whatever to do with this Bill; that it is a question of provincial rights ; that the Manitoba legislature passed the Bill, and that it would not be fair for the parliament of Canada to refuse to ratify it. Indeed, I have heard from very high quarters in this House that this is a case of provincial rights, that Manitoba must be left to work out her own destiny in her own way, and that if she happens to have made a fool of herself, she should be left to take the consequences. I have scarcely found a baker's dozen of the members of this House on either side who have sought in any way to justify the deal. I have found the general impression to be that the deal is an atrocious one, that it is an abominable one, that it is an abominable deal, to use the words of the organ of the Minister of Public Works, as quoted by the hon. member for Winnipeg the other night. I have not found anybody of prominence in the city of Ottawa who is familiar with politics, to offer one word of defence for this measure. And since the transaction, a discussion was had in the Railway Committee, and after it had become absolutely clear that Manitoba is not getting one single thing in return for this vast liability which she is incurring, I have scarcely found anybody at all offer any defence of it whatever. To-night this parliament is called upon, in all solemnity, to ratify this deal. I doubt very gravely whether the hon. member who introduced the Bill, the hon. member for An-tigonish, has ever read it. I would put him the question.
Yes, half a dozen times.

Well, I would like to hear the hon. gentleman tell ns later on what its provisions are. The point I want to make is that this House, under no circumstances, can get rid of its responsibility. It is not a case of provincial rights at all. I think I will be able to prove to the satisfaction of every reasonable man in this House that the Bill we are called on to ratify is in no sense the bargain made between this railway company and the people of Manitoba. I propose to show tonight, in the presence of the ministers-and I am sorry they are not all here-that if they put this Bill through, they are going to be a party to the gold-bricking of Manitoba. They are going to stand sponsor to a deal which is to be forced on the people of Manitoba, and which the people, as represented by the legislature, never agreed to for one moment, and never would. I want to warn the government that Manitoba, which is already saddled with a debt of about SC,000,000, is, in this connection, going to be burdened with a further liability of $17,000,000. I want to show that Manitoba has no resources whatever. You have taken all her lands and given them to railway companies or kept them for yourselves. She

said mortgage securing said issue is to be in a form satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council-
It is important to mark this :
-and to be in similar terms so far as applicable to the mortgage set out in schedule B to chapter 57 of the statutes of Canada for the year 1899, together with such changes and additional clauses as may be necessitated by the terms of this agreement.
Hon. members will see that the reference here is to a mortgage set out in chapter 57 of the statutes of Canada, 1899. That is, these people, Mackenzie & Mann, made an agreement with the Manitoba government some years ago that they should have a guarantee on their railway system from the government of Manitoba of $8,000 a mile, and as security, they gave a first mortgage on all their roads and equipment and appurtenances. Now, the mortgage referred to here is to be in similar terms to that mortgage. My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has made this point and I wish to emphasize it, particularly as the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) are present-that that mortgage should be laid on the Table of the House. The legislature of Manitoba was induced to vote for this contract only on the ground that all these things which were brought up by the board of trade would be provided for in the mortgage. Before we ratify this contract, we should see that mortgage. For the Manitoba legislature will come back at us and say : We only voted for the contract on the understanding that these things would all be provided for in the mortgage ; months have elapsed, and you, the parliament of Canada, ratified this deal without making sure that the things that we were promised were placed in the mortgage. I would like very much if the right hon. the premier-and 1 thank him for his attention-would give us some assurance that he would insist on seeing llmt the whole deal is before us.
To what does my hon. friend refer ?

The railway company gives to the government a first mortgage on its road, the Manitoba system and the Rainy River system. We are going to guarantee $20,000 a mile on the Rainy River Railway. And here is an important thing for the members of the government to remember-that on this very Rainy RiverRailway of 290 miles, we of this parliament granted aid two years ago to the extent of $6,400 a mile, and the government of Ontario granted aid to the extent of $4,000 a mile, making a total of $10,400 a mile.
Only for part of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The important part of it-290 miles. The part from

Fort Francis to Winnipeg is known as the Manitoba South-eastern, and on that the Manitoba government gavo a guarantee of bonds for $S,000 a mile, and the company had also 6,400 acres a mile which would bring them $3 an acre, making over $19,000 a mile, so that on this section they have public aid which would build the road two or three times over. On the Rainy River section there is this $10,400 a mile from the Dominion and from Ontario, and now comes Manitoba giving a guarantee of $20,000 a mile, so that the hvtal aid which the people of Canada are giving on this section is $30,400 a mile. X do not think there is anybody who would contend that that road would cost more than $18,000 a mile equipped. It is true that there are some heavy portions of it, but the average, I think, would not be $18,000 a mile. So, in ratifying this, we have to consider our responsibilities. I would like to call the attention of the minister to this question particularly. He will remember that when that aid was given the hou. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) and myself asked for conditions. We moved for running powers for limitation of the bonds and for control of rates. And this parliament of Canada has control of those rates and control of the running powers on that railway.
Surely, we ought not to allow that company to get $30,400 a mile for building that railway. and that is what they are going to get. That is why I say this legislation is so interwoven with this government that this House could very well pause and say, This is too important a1 matter to be allowed to be rushed through in this way. The point ,1 want to emphasize is that this is not a question of provincial rights, we cannot fold our arms and say, on your heads be the consequences in Manitoba, you are making fools of yourselves-that is the general opinion in this parliament-but you must be permitted to make fools of yourselves. I have liointed out that the ratification of that Bill was only made on the distinct printed agreement that the Lieutenant Governor in Council has power to make such conditions, though the same may be at variance with the contract, as was suggested by the Winnipeg Board of Trade. The Winnipeg Board of Trade appointed a committee to go very carefully into this matter, and they made these recommendations, and on the strength of a distinct agreement that they might be embodied in this contract, the legislature ratified it. But we are ratifying a deal that leaves that out altogether, we are ratifying a deal in which the Minister of Railways and Canals puts a distinct clause that notwithstanding anything in the contract, Canada is going to exercise the control of the rates which she possesses. Now, I am going to be able to satisfy this House that the people of that country never would have ratified the contract under any consideration had they not supposed that Manitoba
was receiving absolute control of the rates, and would be able to fix those rates from time to time.
Now, it was quite clear from the discussion in the Railway Committee and from the position which the Minister of Railways and Canals took in that committee, that the power which Canada has and which she exercises, she cannot remit to Manitoba. The premier was not in the Railway Committee at the time, and for his benefit I propose to make a statement of the case which was made by Mr. Nesbitt, the lawyer for the Committee of Public Safety, who^ has been down here. Under the British North America Act, the Dominion government has exclusive jurisdiction over Dominion railways and can regulate rates. Manitoba now seeks to take that power to herself, and I understand Mr. Nesbitt to take the position that even if you wished, you could not confer upon Manitoba that right. The power you have is conferred upon you by the British North America Act, passed by the Imperial government, and that power you cannot delegate to Manitoba. But Manitoba did not so understand it, Manitoba thought she was getting the absolute right to control these rates, and on that supposition the legislature passed the contract. But it has distinctly come out in this parliament that Manitoba cannot get that power, that the dominion parliament cannot give her that power. Inasmuch as the legislature passed that Act, believing Manitoba could get that power, if you should now ratify the Act, then Manitoba would have a right to hold you responsible and to say that you ratified the Act, knowing the position of affairs, and failed to refer it back to Manitoba. Now, I have a motion to make myself. Although I did not offer any 'protest at the time I was named by the Speaker as seconder to the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg that a plebiscite be taken. I propose to move later on that this Bill should be referred back to the legis-ture of Manitoba, giving them an opportunity to pronounce upon it. Now, I want to read extracts from the speech of Mr. Premier Roblin, for the benefit of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who, I observe, is following my argument closely, and for whose ability as a lawyer I have very great respect. I want to read for his especial benefit an extract from Mr. ROblin's speech on this question, to show him exactly what the understanding was :
Extract from Mr. Roblin's speech at Ne-pawa, February 14th, 1901, as reported in the Morning Telegram of February 15th. The Morning Telegram is the organ of the local government. After the bargain was announced, the premier went up to Nepawa and made a speech in which he announced the terms :
The speaker (Mr. Rovin') was in the legislature at the time, ana although he supported ths

principle of competition, yet for reasons it was unnecessary to go into, he was compelled to oppose the contract by which the Northern Pacific Railway of the United States was to be introduced into Manitoba. The principle of government control of freight rates has been a plank of the platform of the party under Hugh John Macdonald.
In that respect he has not stated the case with perfect accuracy. The principle of Hugh John Macdonald's platform was not so much control of rates as it was a declaration in favour of the government ownership of railroads, and this is not government ownership of railroads that we are getting, we are merely leasing railroads and releasing them to sjpother company, on condition that if the railroad pays then the government will lose nothing, but if the railroad does not pay, the governnment makes up the difference. That is not government ownership of railroads. Mr. Roblin went on to say :
And it was now the speaker's duty and pleasure to finish the work that had been so ably begun. As far as Manitoba was concerned, he believed the transportation question was now solved. Government ownership of railways was but a means to an end, and that end was to secure control of rates, to secure fair and reasonable transportation charges, and one that the people could stand. This was what they had started to work at, and what had now been done.
You see, he says here. What they had started to work out was to secure a control of rates. Now we find out how much control they have got.
The ground had been looked over, and they found they were four or five hundred miles from a point where competition could be had, and where the benefits of competition could be got, and that was Lake Superior.
Then again, in the same speech, speaking of the consideration received by the province :
That means that the people of Manitoba will enjoy a privilege enjoyed by no other province in Canada or state in the United States, that the Lieutenant Governor in Council has the right and authority to make all tariffs from that time forward, until the contract is revoked.
Now, let me tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the Minister of Railways and Canals has put iu this contract a condition that notwithstanding anything in this Bill, this parliament does not divest itself of any power, and discrimination can be prevented, and you can do exactly as you will. Now, if that is so, is it not clear to any reasonable man that Manitoba is not getting what the premier of the province told the people that she was getting And why is she not getting it ? Because we 'are taking it from 'her, and if we are going to take it from her. is it not our bounden duty as public men to say to the people of Manitoba : You have entered into a deal that you did not Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
quite understand, and it is perfectly clear from the contract itself that you did not understand it. In that contract was a provision that Manitoba should have power to make conditions, though they might be at variance with the contract, and we have taken that away.
Surely as honourable men it ought to be our duty to stay our hand for a few weeks and say to the people of Manitoba : We refer this back to you ; if you say, in the face of ay the developments, that you want that deal ratified and that you are willing to take the responsibility of it, then, we will ratify it for you. Then, I want to say, to-night, in all solemnity, that if we force this deal on the people of Manitoba we will have done an act that will reflect the greatest discredit upon the parliament of this country. No greater question has ever been considered by this parliament. No wonder the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair), than whom there is no shrewder man in this House, should stand up, as he did the other day in the Railway Committee, and say : ' I want to warn you that if you pass this deal you are going to have a serious clash between the people of Manitoba and the people of the Dominion and a serious clash between the government of Manitoba and the government of the Dominion.' In the face of these words of the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals, who is charged, and specially charged, to consider this matter, are the members of this parliament, in this Dominion, to be brought into this House to-night to vote this deal down the throats of the people of Manitoba whether they want it or not V Surely, I make a reasonable request, surely I am within my rights in speaking to-night when I ask that you shall stay your hand and say to the people of Manitoba : 'We are willing to allow you to consider this question once more and if, in view of the developments in the Railway Committee and in view of the developments in parliament, you still want that deal to go through, then, and then only, on your heads be it.' I say the people of Manitoba have had no opportunity to consider and discuss this question as they have a right to discuss it. I would not plead, as I do to-night so strongly, did I not know that there is scarcely a man who sits in this parliament of Canada who will stand up and say that this is a good deal. I say that I have heard it denounced from Dan to Beerslieba as an abominable deal, ns a scandal, as a freak, as a thing that is going to ruin the people and the province of Manitoba. If that is so, and if the question is not one of provincial rights, then, I say that the members of this House are in duty bound to pause and consider before they attempt to force this deal upon the people of Manitoba. Now, I want to make a few quotations for the purpose of showing what the people of tlie'province of Manitoba expected to have had from what was ex-

plained to them by their representatives in the legislature and their representatives in the executive government.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson, Lisgar) wanted me to put a contract on the Table. What contract does he refer to ?

No; under this contract there is to be a mortgage given to the province of Manitoba by the company. The province of Manitoba secures a mortgage on the Rainy River Railway. As the right lion, gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) probably knows, this road runs down to Fort Francis on the Rainy River, then runs forty miles through the state of Minnesota, and then again over the river by an international bridge into Ontario from Minnesota. Now, for the vast guarantee which we are giving and which involves a liability of $17,500,000, Manitoba is to get a mortgage on the railway and there is a clause in the original contract which says that the Lieutenant Governor in Council is to be able to make conditions in the mortgage which may be at variance with the contract. The executive said to the legislature : ' We will get all these conditions placed in the mortgage or security that the company gives to the government.' The mortgage is one of the documents to this contract. We ought, at least, if we are bound to push this contract through, to protect the interests of the people of Manitoba. We ought to say to this company :	Place on the Table the
mortgage which you are going to give to the province of Manitoba for this liability which she is going to assume so that parliament may know whether the company is fulfilling the understanding which was arrived at between the legislature and the government and the company. I am glad to observe the interest that the right lion, premier is taking in the matter and I congratulate him upon it, because I know that he does not want to do any wrong act to the people of Manitoba. I fancy that if he thoroughly understands the gravity of this ease he will insist, as it is his duty to insist. that Manitoba shall understand exactly what the conditions of this deal are before it is finally ratified. Why should the bell be rung and lion, members be called in to vote a contract through without understanding absolutely what the conditions are ? Let me read what Premier Roblin said :
That means that the people of Manitoba -will enjoy a privilege enjoyed by no other province in Canada or state in the United States, that the Lieutenant Governor in Council has the right and authority to make all tariffs from that time .upward until the contract is revoked.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies), I am sure, will be interested to know that it came out clearly and distinctly in the Railway Committee that notwithstanding any of these things, Manitoba has no more power than she ever had, that you cannot give her more power and that there is no way in which she can be seized of more power. If this is true, what becomes of Premier Roblin's statement ? We should not blind ourselves with the idea that we can justly, as honourable men, ratify a contract of that nature. We cannot do it. We are deceiving ourselves. It will be a lasting disgrace to the parliament of Canada if it is done, because it will be done in the face of the facts being plainly pointed out and laid before the people of Canada. Here is another utterance of Premier Roblin in the same speech :
The country might, he felt, look forward with confidence to the future, as this railway policy would be the inauguration of a new era of prosperity and growth, particularly in an agricultural sense that would be a wonder

I want the House specially to mark the language that the premier uses. He speaks to the legislature and the people of Manitoba of the wonderful revolution that is going to occur, of the marvels that are going to take place in the development of the country. Mark his language, and when the House understands that the province of Manitoba has not one iota now that it had not before it will see what a farce we are enacting in ratifying a contract of this description. He says :
The country might, he felt, look forward with confidence to the future, as this railway policy would be the inauguration of a new era of prosperity and growth, particularly in an agricultural sense, that would be a wonder and a marvel to other parts of Canada, because of confidence that would be established by the fact that the government, the people, controlled the rates, would be an encouragement to the farmers to increase the area of the land they cultivated, and their herds, and show the enterprise and development that a flourishing condition of things will warrant.
He was practically preaching a new gospel to the people of Manitoba, giving them to understand that when a deal like this went through it would be a land flowing with milk and honey. Manitoba is not going to be placed in any better position than she was iu prior to the making of this contract. I world like to get the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to this point. W.e have a provision, as he knows, in the Railway Act, allowing the Governor General in Council to fix the rates on Canadian railways. Let us consider for a moment this point.
On what basis are the rates to be fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council ? Is the company to be allowed working expenses and interest on capital invested ? Would you allow them bigli interest on stock, or would you allow them large profits ? Tlie point I want to make is :	That inasmuch as Canada has

already aided tUis road to the extent of $10,400 a mile, and Manitoba is now being gold-bricked into giving it $20,000 a mile, why should we not in all conscience exercise control of the rates. 1 remember how well that point was discussed by the member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) when that aid went through. If we gave that company all that aid and if we took power to control their rates, in the name of reason why should not the rates be controlled on that road, and why should we be asked to-night to vote a farcial bargain through, and lead Manitoba into a debt of over seventeen and a half million dollars, in order that Manitoba may get a control which she does not really get, but which we already have and which we ought now exercise ? It seems to me that my proposition is so fair, so plain, so reasonable, that I marvel there is not an outcry against this Bill. I say to hou. gentlemen:	You cannot fold your
arms and laugh it off and say, it is Manitoba's business, and if Manitoba wants to ruin herself, let her. That won't do. As serious men sent here by our constituents, we have to consider this point and if we have paid already, and paid almost the cost of the road to get control of the rates, why should we not exercise that control without allowing poor Manitoba to ruin herself in order to get a so-called control which does not amount to the snap of your fingers ? Here is an extract from an editorial in the Winnipeg Telegram, the organ of the local government, dated February 15 :
No matter how critically the contracts are examined, no interpretation can be put upon them which can take away from the people of Manitoba the control of the rates.
Let the Minister of Railways mark that. He stated in the Railway Committee with perfect frankness that no matter what Manitoba may do she gets no more control than she had before.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Manitoba may, if she chooses work with the company, but the government of Canada is in no way divested of its control and can interfere. That is what the Minister of Railways said. This paper continues :
The object of government ownership of railways, commissions, and all .other methods of public regulation is the control of the rates, and this the government has secured in the most direct form.
I claim that the government has secured nothing of the kind.
The rates are to he fixed by the Lieutenant
Governor in Council.
Here is an extract from another editorial in the same paper of February IS :
The government has no jurisdiction over Jnited States lines, and cannot determine their Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
rates, but there will always be competition up to the boundary, and within the province the government can make the rates what is pleases.
It came out in the Railway Committee the other day, that if the government makes a low rate In Manitoba and if a higher rate prevails in Ontario on the connecting system, the Dominion government can step in and raise the rates in Manitoba. We have the power to equalize the rates and we cannot divest ourselves of that power. If any complaint is made of discrimination, that the rates are higher in Ontario than in Manitoba, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council must take cognizance of that complaint and must raise the rates in Manitoba to be equal to the rates on the connections in Ontario and the North-west Territories. That being the case, Manitoba gets nothing. She assumes a liability of $17,500,000 in order that she may limit the rates to any figure she likes within her own province. She expects that the rates shall be higher in the Territories and in Ontario, in order that the company may earn sufficient money elsewhere to raise their general revenues, but if the parliament of Canada, through the Railway Committee of the Privy Council is going to step in and raise the rates in Manitoba, then Manitoba receives absolutely nothing for the $17,500,000 which she assumes. Is this parliament going to ratify this contract with its eyes open ? This newspaper continues :
This is all the safeguard that can possibly he asked. There is no loop-hole for the company. They would have no object whatever in charging higher rates on freight from any point in Ontario on their lines to the borders of Manitoba, for the simple reason that the higher rates would appear in their income, and would give the government an excuse to cut off other rates.
They have in mind that if the rates are high in Ontario and in the Territories, they will be earning so much money that tlie Manitoba government can Immediately cut the rates and consequently get some benefit from this enormous liability. But it came out in the Railway Committee the other day that the Dominion government could at once raise the rates in Manitoba, and consequently Manitoba does not receive the least consideration for tlie enormous liability she has assumed. The extracts which I am reading are short and I know they 'will not weary the House, because I wish to present the case as fairly and as clearly ns I can, in order that it might be understood, and I will endeavour to be as concise as possible Another editorial from the same paper of February 19, says :
We are convinced that the result of all the study and criticisms now being devoted to the bargin will be to confirm the people in their first judgment Nothing can possibly destroy the original impression that the government has actually secured control of the rates. This

control is as absolute as if the government operated the lines itself.
Wliat does tlie Minister of Railways think of that statement, that the control of Manitoba over the rates is absolute. An editorial note in the same paper of February 20, says :
The government will fix the rates, not only on wheat, salt and coal, but on every kind of freight.
Here is another editorial from the same paper of February 21:
Rates on Rainy River District.
The question has evidently been raised in some minds whether the government will have control of rates between Manitoba points and points in the Rainy River districts. Certainly the government will be able to control these rates. The company could have no possible motive for even attempting to charge more than the standard of government rates for that class of transportation. If it raised the rates from some point in the Rainy River district to the borders of Manitoba the government would lower the rates within the province. If it made a large profit on the Rainy River branch there would be less need for a large income in other portions. In a fight of that kind the company would be certain to lose. It cannot make a cent of profit over and above fixed charges unless the people of Manitoba allow it to do so. To antagonize the people in a hopeless struggle would be the most senseless thing the company could do. The people have the situation in their hands.
Let me explain that there are forty miles of this railway running through the state of Minnesota. How is the government of Manitoba to control rates in the state of Minnesota ? Then, there is an international bridge connecting the state of Minnesota with the province of Ontario, which has been organized under the laws of the state of Minnesota ; and under this lease this company could charge exactly what it liked on that connecting link, and how could the government of Manitoba, or any Canadian government, control rates or working expenses there ? It may be said that the company will act in good faith. We do not know that, and it is our business to absolutely safeguard that point, and to see, even if the Manitoba government has not been wise in the matter, that the people of Manitoba are going to be protected. Here is another brief extract from the same paper on February 25 :
Is the principle of government control of rates the right principle ? The people of Manitoba have had experience of the other principle. Are they satisfied to have that other principle remain in force ? If the present opportunity is lost no other may be found within the life of this generation. This will be no excuse for accepting a positively bad bargain but this is not a bad bargain. The company gives up to the government all its right over rates.
The company may fancy that it is giving to the government of Manitoba all rights over rates, but the government of Canada
possesses the rights which it has always exercised, and it cannot divest itself of those rights. Here is an extract from a speech of Premier Roblin, before the Winnipeg Board of Trade, as reported in the organ of the Manitoba government, on February 27 :
They (the government) laid down the principle that the government should control the rates ; they adhered to it and eventually secured it for them. If it was not a desirable thing for the province to get control of the freight rates on wheat the contract was wrong.
This is-a very important statement of the premier. I will make it much clearer before I get through that Manitoba is not getting control of rates, aud cannot exercise complete control. I read again :
If it was improper for the people's representatives to reduce the tariffs for merchandise he admitted they had made a mistake. But he did not interpret the mandate received by those in office at the present time to be to that effect. Consequently when they had established or got the principle recognized by the corporations they undertook to secure that principle, protect it as far as possible, and much such assurances that it would be effective. If the government had left anything out, left anything undone that ought to have been done, in order to secure that, they would be only too glad to have suggestions on that subject.
Now, a committee of the board of trade was appointed to confer with Mr. Roblin and his government. That committee consisted of, I think, twelve of the ablest members of the board of trade. They were to go through the contract and make suggestions, and it was represented that the suggestions of the board of trade would be adopted. Consequently many members of the board of trade were willing to agree to the contract under the belief that their suggestions would be adopted ; but they were not adopted, and nothing of importance was done with regard to them. At the same meeting, Mr. Roblin referred to an alternative proposition which had been made about the same time by the Canadian Pacific Railway. It offered to give the government practically the same control of rates that was obtained in. this case ; that is, if any complaint were made with regard to rates, the matter was to be referred to the King's Bench, and evidence taken ; and unless the company could show that the rate which the government made was too low a rate, then that rate would prevail. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company offered certain specific reductions which would bring the rate on wheat from Manitoba to Lake Superior from 14 cents per hundred pounds down by a sliding scale, until in two or three years it reached 10 cents per hundred pounds. They also offered to build any reasonable extensions which the province might require to accommodate the people, and asked for no guarantee whatever. I think it was generally admitted that

the offer of the Canadian Pacific Kailway Company was just as valuable, probably more valuable than the offer of this company, because the Canadian Pacific Railway was willing to give these reductions, and asked for nothing in return. It was. of course, going to take over the Northern Pacific system on practically the same terms ; but there has been a strong feeling of hostility to the Canadian Pacific Railway in that country for many years, due very largely to the arrogant policy which that company pursued. I need not offer to hon. members any evidence of that feeling ; they see ebulitions of it in this House from time to time. The government took this view-and I am disposed to think that in so doing they accurately gauged public opinion-that if the bargain which the Canadian Pacific Railway offered was a better one. they dared not ask the legislature to ratify it. because to hand over any provincial franchise into the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway would raise a great outcry in the province. That was the argument used by the government and tlie legislature of Manitoba why the offer of the Canadian Pacific Railway should be rejected and that of the Canadian Northern Railway accepted. Let me continue reading the extract. I am not sure where I finished reading-
Begin it again.

I do not like to hear remarks of that kind, because they would seem to imply that I am simply endeavouring to take up the time of the House, whereas I am, in all gravity and sincerity, trying to the best of my poor ability
Oh, oh.

I hear again some of these hoarse laughs that were won't to resound in the committee whenever the interests of the people were advocated against the interests of a corporation. What difference does it make to these hon. gentlemen if Manitoba should sink deeper than the lost continent of Atlantas ? If Manitoba chooses to make a fool of herself, let her do so. They would rather take the side of the .corporation than that of the people, who are bound to be dragged down to provincial ruin if this deal be ratified. That is the position I take, and while I do not wish to be at all offensive, I think it but right that, in response to these interruptions, I should reiterate that I am trying, to the best of my limited ability, to present this case, and it is very gratifying to me to find that there are many members who are listening very earnestly to the argument I am making.
Go on.
I propose to go on in my own way, and I wish to say, in the mildest manner possible, that while I am not at all desirous of doing anything the House may disapprove of

Hon. Mr. PRIOR, I merely asked the hon. gentleman to read over again what he had read before. He said that he had read only a small portion, and 1 do not see why he should take up the time of the House by giving expression to his umbrage at an imaginary slight.
There was an imputation in that remark
You are a little too touchy.

Perhaps I am, but I want the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., to understand that I am not the least bit angry and hope he will not misunderstand me. I merely wish to enter a very mild protest

So I intend. I continue reading from Mr. Roblin's speech:
Having secured the lease of the Northern Pacific, the government made up their minds as to what they wanted from the Canadian Northern. They stated that they wanted absolute control of the freight rates. The Canadian Northern were not willing to give this without considerable argument.
That is what the First Minister of Manitoba said :
They (the company) wished to establish a fixed rate, say 10 cents on wheat, taking Brandon as a centre, and 20 per cent reduction on the tariff of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as it then existed. The government, however, would not accept that as what then appeared a reasonable rate might in five or ten years be an exorbitant one, therefore it was better to have absolute control.
These are the premier's own words. The Telegram, which is the organ of the government, on March 29th, gave this extract from the speech of the First Minister of the province at an entertainment given by the Young Men's Conservative Association :
The Dominion parliament had the power to do so (veto), hut he hoped and believed that they would not do so. The Dominion would not be justified in depriving the government of this opportunity to get control of freight rates, unless the Dominion was prepared to spend money to alleviate the freight rates disadvantage under which the province now suffered.
I would ask the attention of the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies) to this opinion of the Attorney General of the province. In the Telegram of March 9tli, Attorney General Campbell is reported as having said on tlie previous evening, in reply to Mr. Myers :
It is the intention of the government that the government will absolutely control the rates, and that rates will be fixed so that no one but the Lieutenant Governor in Council will be able to dispute them.
That was the position taken by the legal adviser of the Crown, the Attorney General.

It is pretty clear wliat lie understood. I wish now to read from the Edmonton Bulletin, a paper, which, I believe, is owned by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). The opinion I am about to read is pretty significant, in view of the position which that hon. gentleman takes in favour of this contract. In the Edmonton Bulletin of February 25th, 1901, there appears this leading article : The Canadian Northern gives 3 cents a mile passenger rate over all its lines within the province, and hands over absolutely to the control of the province for a period of thirty years the freight rates from point to point within the province and between provincial points and Port Arthur. If these are the words of the hon. member- and he will no doubt contradict me if they are not-his view was that the province got absolute control over freight rates. The Bulletin continues : The Manitoba government, by assuming responsibility for the interest on the cost of the road, becomes entitled to fix the rates to be charged. This is fair to the investors, whose money built the railways, and who do not care where their interest comes from, so long as it comes ; and it is fair to the people of the province, who can claim rates to suit themselves, so long as the interest payments are kept up from whatever source. The control that has been secured in Manitoba must be secured in the Territories. I want to call especial attention to this : Manitoba has set the pace and the Territories will demand equal advantages when the time comes. What does that mean ? It means that Manitoba, having assumed a liability of seventeen and a half million dollars, to obtain the control of freight rates in Manitoba, the Territories must get similar control. Then, why should Manitoba be called on to assume an immense liability in order that, not only Manitoba, but the Territories as well should get low freight rates ? This accounts for the stand taken by the hon. member for Alberta in favour of this Bill. We can understand then why we hear no voice but the voice of acclaim in favour of this deal from all the members from the North-west Territories. Because if the dictum of the Edmonton Bulletin be true, if the Territories are going to get exactly the same rates as Manitoba, without paying a cent, then there is a great advantage to the Territories in this agreement. The House will clearly understand why the members of the Territories should fold their arms and say : Well, this is none of our funeral. Manitoba is assuming a liability of seventeen and a half million dollars, and if she gets low freight rates so do we. and therefore we say hurrah for the ratification of the Bill. 1 think that hon. members should bear this point very strongly in mind when they recognize that the voice of the North-west Territories	is in favour of the ratification of this deal. True, we might have expected them to show some patriotism ; true, we might have expected these hon. gentlemen to say-as I am confident most of them believe-that since this deal spells ruin to the province of Manitoba, and since Manitoba did not know- what she was doing when she agreed to it, we will come to her relief ; but their interest appears to blind them to every other consideration, and when they are led to believe that they will get the same rates without making any sacrifice, we are prepared to vote this measure through, cost what it may to a neighbouring province. Another brief extract from the Edmonton Bulletin and I will close the reading of extracts showing what was said with regard to the fixing of rates. This is from the Edmonton Bulletin of March 8th : The people of Manitoba have the game in their own hands, and it is for them to play it or to say that they do not want what they have been shouting for during the past fifteen years	 Mark the words

 -definite and permanent control of railway rates. Now, have they got or are they going to get definite and permanent control of rates ? I do not think that there is any member within the sound of my voice who believes that they are going to get anything of the kind. Now, not being a practised speaker, I have-always found some difficulty in arranging my speech consecutively. I am apt to follow one particular line away from an argument that I wish to pursue. I will ask the House therefore to go back to where I started.
