Any overdue coupons on the bonds so delivered shall, before delivery, be cut off and cancelled. fix the rates to be charged or demanded by the company for the carriage of all freight from all points on the company's lines in Manitoba to Port Arthur, and from Port Arthur to all points on the company's lines in Manitoba, and from all points on the company's lines in Manitoba to all other points on said lines in Manitoba. Provided always, that before any rates are so fixed, the company shall be heard and their interests taken into consideration. The company agrees that it will not at any time after the said rates have been so fixed charge or demand for the carriage of freight between the points aforesaid greater rates than those so fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Thus the company agree that it shall never charge higher rates than the rates fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council. But now, when we come to the contract wnich we are ratifying, it is clearly understood that this parliament can exercise its control of rates ; and if the rates in Manitoba are lower than in Ontario or the North-west Territories, this parliament can direct the equalization of those rates notwithstanding anything that is here stipulated. If a railway commission for the Dominion is appointed-and we are given to understand that we shall have a railway commission-does any one suppose that that commission will allow a low rate in Manitoba and a high rate in Ontario or the North-west Territories. As was shown on the committee, they will call for the equalization of rates. Therefore, this clause of the contract falls :

The company hereby consents to the passing of such legislation by the legislature of Manitoba as may be necessary to confer upon the Court of King's Bench for Manitoba full jurisdiction at the instance of the Attorney General of the province on behalf of the government, to decree specific performance and observance by the company of each and every of the terms of this agreement, and of the said lease and option, and the company hereby consents to and submits to the jurisdiction of the said court in that behalf.	i

10.	Commencing when this agreement takes effect, the company shall reduce its passenger rates in Manitoba to not exceeding 3 cents per passenger per mile.
I am under the impression that we have a three-cent rate in Manitoba already. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) nods his head and acquiesces in that opinion. He is a better authority than I am on that point, and so hon. members will see that this clause of the contract is practically of no value.
11.	The receipts and income of the company from operating the lines of railway included in the mortgage securing said guaranteed bonds and from all its lines in Manitoba, including the lines demised by said leases and option, shall be applied in the first place in payment of the working expenditure of said lines of railway, and in the second place in payment of the rentals under said lease and option and interest on bonds on said lines heretofore or hereafter guaranteed by the government or issued with the consent of the government.
They have to pay working expenses first, then rentals under the lease, and then interest on bonds.
Now. how are we going to control the working expenses on the forty miles iu Minnesota ? We have no control over that. Is there any member of this House who, if he makes a contract with anybody, does not stipulate in the bond exactly what can and cannot be done ? This forty miles in Minnesota begins under foreign control, and how are we to tell what the working expenses may be in a foreign country ? The company can do exactly as it likes there, and we can exercise no control. So, if they are able to charge what they like for working expenses, the House must see that the province of Manitoba has no chance of getting the rental paid. And that brings us back to the old proposition, that unless this parliament takes care absolutely to safeguard these bonds and to see that the company is going to be able to pay interest and rentals, then we are going to have repudiation. Manitoba cannot pay it. that is clear. Her expenditure yearly is greater than her revenue, and that being the case, she has got to go on borrowing, and after a while she will get to the end of her tether, and she will come down and ask this parliament, who forced this contract on her, to pay her liabilities.
And in consideration of said power given to the Lieutenant Governor in Council respecting | the fixing of rates, the government agrees that if the said receipts and income, after payment of said working expenditure, are not sufficient to pay said rentals and interest, the deficiency (if any) shall be borne by the government, and the company shall be relieved therefrom. Provided always, that the said deficiency (if any) shall be ascertained at the end of each period of two years, commencing from the 1st day of October. 1901, and any surplus in either year of any such period shall, as far as necessary, be I applied in reduction of any deficiency in the

other year of said period; but each period of two years shall for the purpose of this clause be treated apart from each other period.
They divide it into periods of two years, and if the road pays in any two-year periods, then they pay the rental ; but, if it loses, the goverhemnt pays the rental. If, however, there should be a large surplus in this two years period, and if the company should make far more money than would pay the working- expenses, rentals and interest on the bonds, then, they put the surplus into their pockets. But, if there are two lean years, the government has got to suffer, the government has got to pay any loss in the lean years. But, if there are two fat years all the company does is to pay the rentals, add to put the rest of the money in their pockets. That clause has been strongly objected to as a jug-handled clause. In fact, any legal gentleman who will go through that contract will find that it is a case of heads I win for the company, and tails you lose for the province.
For the purposes of this clause the term ' working expenditure ' shall not include the salary or remuneration of any officer, employee or other person whose time is not wholly employed bona fide in connection with the said lines of railways in this clause mentioned ; but as to officers and employees and other persons whose services are necessary or desirable in connection with the said lines and whose whole time is not taken up in connection therewith there shall be Included reasonable remuneration for the time .aotually expended and services actually rendered by them in connection with said lines; and the said term shall not include any expenses, payments or outgoings not reasonably necessary for the efficient management, maintenance, operation and repair of the said lines, nor shall the said term include the cost of double tracking the said lines, but siding reasonably required for the traffic and operation of the lines shall not be deemed double tracking. Should any dispute arise between the government and the company as to working expenditure under this clause, the same shall be referred to the chief justice of the Court of King's Bench for Manitoba for the time being, who shall have full power to decide the same, and in so deciding he may take evidence or consult with experts, and use his own judgment in coming to a decision, and his decision shall be final and binding and without appeal. For the purposes of this clause the Minnesota and Manitoba Railway shall be deemed to be a line of railway included in the said mortgage securing said guaranteed bonds.
That might appear as if the Minnesota section were brought under the operation of this Act ; but, you will realize that you cannot make subject to the jurisdiction of any Canadian court a company which is organized in the United States, and whose operations are confined to the United States.

The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou-rassa) made a strong argument in the Railway Committee on that very point. The company under this contract must build a road from its Rainy River line down to Duluth, and later on the company may, for reasons of its own, choose to send all its freight by Duluth. Then, what becomes of control in the Dominion ? The Dominion may say : You must not send that freight over the American line of railway, we insist that it he sent over the Canadian railway ; and the company may say : Well, that makes quite a difference, and if you insist on that we shall be unable to carry out our contract with Manitoba. maintopic: FULL TEXT OF THE ACT RATIFYING CANADIAN NORTHERN CONTRACT, AS IT PASSED THE MANITOBA LEGISLATURE, MARCH 13.
speechtext:
1 do not despair that I will convince the right hon. gentleman before I finish. On the suggestion of the Minister of Railways, the following was added to the Bill :
Nothing In this Act or in the indenture in the schedules hereto contained, or done in pursuance of this Act or of the said indenture shall first : (a) Divest or limit temporarily or otherwise the rights or powers under existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada, of the government or the Governor General in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or of any commissioner or other authority respecting any matter or any obligation or duty.
We are not giving to Manitoba the Act they passed, but we distinctly declare that the Dominion of Canada is going to exercise its power as in the past.
(b) Place the Governor of Canada directly or indirectly under any liability, obligation or duty with respect to any bonds debentures stocks or securities of any kind or any interest thereon, or any payment mentioned in the said indenture Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
provided for or referred to or in any way arising therefrom. (c) Authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company contrary to the meaning of the Railway Act to charge or demand any higher rates for the carriage of freight or passengers than those ^ heretofore or hereinafter fixed under the authority of existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada, by the Governor General in Council or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or by any commissioner or other authority.
I cannot see, for the life of me, that this is not inconsistent with the bargain contained in the agreement of the 11th of February, 1901. It is certainly not the contract which was made between the Manitoba legislature and the Canadian Northern Railway Company. By paragraph 5 of said agreement of the 11th of February, 1901 :
The said mortgage securing said issue is to be in a form satisfactory to the Lieutenant Governor in Council and to be in similar terms so far as applicable to the mortgage set out in schedule B to chapter 57 of the statutes of Canada for the year 1899 together with such changes and additional clauses as may be necessitated by the terms of such agreement.
You see again that is a strong argument in favour of the production of the contract. It is to be on terms similar to the mortgage which was executed in 1899 between the province of Manitoba and these same railway people. I have that mortgage here in the statutes, and may at a later stage read it to the House, in order that when we do get the mortgage in this case we may be able to see that it is in similar terms. Under the clause which I read, the Lieutenant Governor in Council was empowered to change any of the provisions of the bargain ; and, as I pointed out, there was a specific change made in the bargain between the parties. In Bill No. 103, as originally submitted to the parliament of Canada, section 2 provided for the inclusion of such specific change or any other change which the Lieutenant Governor in Council might deem necessary. The language was as follows :
The company may, in the mortgage securing the bonds mentioned in paragraph five of the said indenture, agree to such terms to amplify and carry out the provisions of the said indenture and such other term as the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of Manitoba may deem necessary in the public interests, though they may be at variance with any of the provisions of the said indenture.
That, of course, we are not ratifying. The parliament of Canada is not being asked to carry out the wishes of the legislature of Manitoba, as set forth in their legislation, but, on the contrary, is being asked to enable the railway company to enter into a bargain which has not been endorsed by the legislature of Manitoba. That point I have amplified.
Now, I would like to present in brief form the objections which are made to the agreement by a large section of the people of Manitoba, as represented by a delegation

which appeared here within the last week or two, the members of which were heard before the Railway Committee. That delegation has analysed these contracts, and has brought out in bold relief the main points of objection, and it is important that the House should be seized of these. The member for Winnipeg has, I think, submitted to the House evidence which ought to satisfy reasonable people that the great majority of the people of Manitoba are against the ratification of this deal. These are the points of objection made by the delegation to which I have referred :
The government of the province of Manitoba have agreed to lease from the Northern Pacific Railway Company their lines in that province for nine hundred and ninety-nine years at an annual rental charge of $210,000 for the first ten years, $225,000 for the second ten years, $275,000 for the third ten years, and $300,000 for the balance of the period. The province has also the option of purchase any time for $7,000,000.
By agreement (see Appendix ' A ') the government assigns this lease and option to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, guarantees the bonds, interests, and principal, on 290 miles of the latter company's lines in the province of Ontario, and permits a further issue of $2,000 a mile on their lines in Manitoba.
The province is therefore primarily liable for an annual charge of (1) $298,000 average annual rental; (2) $232,000 interest on bonds on Ontario section; (3) $153,920 interest on bonds formerly guaranteed by the province on Canadian Northern Railway lines in Manitoba ; making a total annual charge of $683,920, and a capital liability of $17,610,000.
These figures are alarmingly great, and while we believe the transportation problem in the province requires attention, the liability assumed under these contracts is entirely out of proportion to the benefits to be derived from them.
The total revenue of the province is about $900,000, and the expenditure approximately the same.
I think that is a mistake. My impression is that the total revenue of the province barely exceeds $700,000, and the expenditure is approximately the same. Indeed, it is generally greater, there being usually a deficit.
It will be seen, therefore, that an additional annual charge, part or all of which we may be called upon to pay-and under certain conditions the railway company are relieved from repayment-is a dangerous experiment, and a risk our young province has no right to take.
The right of municipalities to bonus enterprises by popular vote was some years ago abolished by the legislature, because of the serious results already experienced by several municipalities, yet the legislature, without giving an opportunity for expression by the people, proposes to bonus a railway enterprise by a guarantee of bonds. Is it not fair to ask that the province be given reasonable time to consider a proposition involving a liability of over $400 on each farmer in Manitoba ?
The consideration named in clause 8 of the contract is problematical, indefinite and unsatisfactory to the people. ' Control of rates ' is a 141
vague term and may mean much, little or no benefit to the province. In the first place the government, every year, face a fixed charge of over $600,000, a circumstance in itself to influence rates, then crop conditions, good or bad times, competition and many other things might operate, so that the government before they can control rates are themselves controlled by circumstances that may render them powerless. In view of the very substantial assistance given we think it reasonable to demand that maximum rates should be named.
The contracts were first made public February 16th, and ratified by the legislature March 13th inst.-just twenty-five days. The conditions in the country do not justify this haste. We speak for a vast majority of the province when we urge upon parliament the importance of delay. If the contract is good, delay cannot injure it, if it is bad delay by parliament will do our young province infinite service.
The* provincial securities and guaranteed bonds already afloat amount in round figures to $5,000,000. This sum should not be increased unless it is absolutely certain that corresponding benefits would follow. This proposal will increase our liability to about $20,000,000, a sum certainly alarming considering that our total population does not exceed 300,000. We hope for the contrary, but it seems reasonable to expect that this enormous liability will injuriously affect every security-local or provincial-which may in the future be offered for sale.
No provision is made for future railway extension. Many sections of the province are still suffering for want of railway facilities. These sections are liable for their share of the liability and should be considered in the contracts.
That is the point I sought to make at the outset. We do not ask much ; we merely ask you to vote the question hack to Manitoba, in view of the changed conditions, and in view of the definite statement that Manitoba is not getting what she thought she was getting. It is only fair to say to Manitoba, we will give you another chance to think it over, and then if you ratify it, it will be reasonable to allow it to go. So far as I am concerned, I would then withdraw any opposition I have to the ratification now. No provision is made for future railway extension. Many sections of the province are still suffering for want of railway facilities, and these sections are liable for their share and should be considered in the contract.
In this contract there is no provision made for railway extension, but in the offer submitted by the Canadian Pacific Railway there was provision for a number of desirable railway extensions in the province :
There is no provision in the contract governing rates on construction material. As the construction company and the railway company are practically the same, the rate should be fixed so that construction material would not be hauled at a loss. *
Two other offers were made to the government by responsible corporations, which offers carried with them specific and satisfactory reduction in rates, one imposed no liability, and the other a much less onerous amount. In view of these facts, we think tt is reasonable



to claim that delay in ratifying the Canadian Northern contract might open up a way to a satisfactory settlement of the transportation problem, and perhaps save us from a perilous position.
In this connection we might observe that even after the lease and contracts were made public, responsible parties have offered to build and equip a line of railway equal in length and of the same standard as the Northern Pacific for the sum of $3,500,000 or $10,000 per mile, just half the sum at which the value is fixed in the agreement.
That is the important point, but notwithstanding the fact that Manitoba is paying to the Northern Pacific Railway $7,01)0,000, a responsible company has offered to duplicate these lines for just half that amount. Let me read a letter sent to the Tribune and addressed to the Winnipeg Telegraiy. the local government organ :
To the Editor of the Tribune.
Dear Sir,

Will you kindly give space in the Tribune to the inclosed letter which I have forwarded to the Telegram :
To the Editor of the Telegram.
Sir,-In your issue of the 23rd I notice you state as follows :-
' It is observable that those who are criticising -the government's solution of the railway problem have no suggestions to offer as to what course should be taken by the government.'
As I have been hauled into this controversy somewhat against my will, I looked upon this as a challenge. I wish to say I am friendly to the present government, and would dislike very much to see a change at the present moment. There are members supporting the ratification of this contract with the Canadian Northern whom I have known from their boyhood, and I cannot point to a single discreditable transaction by them, and while I criticise the contract I want to do it in the utmost fairness, with all possible consideration to the men who are personal friends of mine. I think our principal difference is, they are more sanguine in the possibilities in the future than I am and they have less knowledge of the cost of railway construction than I have.
I will just mention a few points that will grow more difficult to explain as the business men of the country have time to look into them. We will consider the question of the purchase of -the railway from the Northern Pacific. I looked up a railway manual and found that the Northern Pacific cost about $21,000 a mile when they had 250 miles built; that is for rolling stock and everything, excepting the big Manitoba Hotel. I must confess I cannot account for $3,000 a mile of this cost. I do not think it was ever put in the road, because neither the iron on that road, nor the roiling stock would indicate any such cost. I have gone into the cost of roads all over this prairie country, and I find the highest cost was the Northern Pacific up to the date of building 250 miles, and the lowest was the Pipestone branch, which did not, cost $6,000 a mile. We" know that the rolling stock on these branches is worth very little, many of the cars and engines being small and old, and it is a question whether it is better to run these old, light engines into the lake and drown them, or to continue doing business with them. As to the cost of rolling stock, Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
$500 Cl- $600 a mile will obtain the rolling stock of many of the branch lines in Manitoba, and with the average branch line such as the Northern Pacific in Manitoba we have ample evidence to show, a nice profit can he made in this prairie country at $10,000 a mile.
I offer to-day to put up a quarter of a million dollars security with the provincial government, in any hands that they may name, satisfactory to us, that I will build the line mile for mile, with station and roiling stock, for the 350 miles of railroad owned by the Northern Pacific in Manitoba for $10,000 a mile. I will have this road ready for hauling out the wheat crop next fall, and I am sure the country does not require a road to haul wheat before that; for although there are many roads running into this country, there is little wheat to haul now. I will build it in every particular as good as the Northern Pacific, only if I enter into the contract in the near future I would require the privilege of putting in sawn ties, which I cannot obtain from the saw-mills, as it would be impossible to take out new ties this season. That would amount to $3,500,000 for the road that the government propose to pay $7,000,000 or 100 per cent more than the cost of a new road.
Here is a man in Manitoba, Captain William Robinson, worth from half a million to a million dollars, who offers to put up with the government $250,000 as security that lie will duplicate this line of railway for just one-half what the province is paying. The House will understand the great desirability of getting a road as cheaply as possible because the company has to earn the interest on the amount invested by the government, and if not the government must make up the deficiency. If, therefore, the capitalization is limited to three million and a half instead of seven million dollars, it must be clear that it would be very much easier to make up tlie interest.
I will not read the balance of Mr. Robinson's letter although he goes into the question very fully, but I merely wanted to make his offer clear. I now continue to give the objections offered by the Citizens Committee :
As further evidence of excessive capitalization, we may mention that Mr. Mellen, president of the Northern Pacific Railway Company, agreed ito enter into a partnership arrangement, putting in the same property at $5,265,000, and this sum is $1,000,000 in excess of the cost, as shown by the railway manual.
The premier of Manitoba agreed to amend the contract, by making It clear that the Canadian Northern Railway should not be relieved of any deficit until the grain rate to Port Arthur had been reduced below 10 cents per 100 pounds, and a greater reduction than 15 per cent below present rates on merchandise, but the amending Aot is so worded that the company will be relieved of any deficit if either one or the other of these reductions is made. If, for instance, a reduction of 16 per cent is made on merchandise, the wheat rate might remain as at present (14 cents) and the company he relieved foom any deficit.
The consideration to the provinoe is provided in clause 8 of the contract. Premier Roblin and Attorney General Campbell have insisted in and out of the House that it gives .the power

to fix freight rates to cover only working expenses and fixed charges. There is no doubt their supporters were influenced by these explanations. Eminent counsel doubt the right of the Dominion parliament to delegate to the government of Manitoba power to fix rates, and even if such power exists, the wording of the clause limits the reduction by requiring not only that the working expenses and fixed charges be provided for, but that the interests of the company shall be conslderd; thus clearly providing for a dividend on the stock of the company-notwithstanding the interpretation of the Attorney General that ' this clause means only that the government shall be courteous.'
Clause 11 of the contract provides that time shall be divided into two-year periods, and that the profits of one period shall not be liable for the profits of another. This is a most unfair arrangement, as all the profits are to be enjoyed by one of the partners to the agreement, and all the losses borne by the other. Clause 11 also attempts to define the meaning of the term ' working expenses.' In our view the definition is absurdly favourable to the company. Everything short of double tracking may be charged to working expenses, and as it is provided that sidings shall not be deemed double tracks, the inference is that sidings, ballasting, station houses, indeed everything but double tracks will be charged to expense account, rendering it reasonably certain that funds will be so used which should be set aside to pay interest and rental charges. We might add that the light rails now on the line will in the very near future be replaced by heavier ones; there is nothing in this contract to prevent the company charging this item also to working expenses.
Clause 14 provides that an auditor shall be appointed by the company with the approval of the government. In our opinion the auditor should be a permanent official, and should hold office during the pleasure of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, and should make sworn returns.
Under the contract the government will not be represented on the railway board. It is fair to demand that when the province furnishes practically all the credit, that it should hold, in trust at least, 51 per cent of the railwav stock.
I tliink that is a reasonable proposition.
Why should the province of Manitoba be obliged at so great a risk and cost to again purchase from Canadian Northern Railway Company the right to fix the rates, when the parliament of Canada has already secured this right in the interests of the people of Canada in consideration of financial assistance granted to the company ?
That is exactly the point I made.
Surely it is not necessary to again buy this right to make the bargain between the company and the parliament of Canada effective.
J. H. BROCK, Winnipeg.
D. W. BOLE, Winnipeg.
A. C. FRASER, Brandon.
EDW. BROWN, Portage la Prairie.
WM. ROBINSON, Selkirk.
I might add that John Arbuthnot, mayor of Winnipeg, was one of the delegation who appeared before the Railway Committee and presented the case. Now, I just want to complete this argument by pointing out, 141*
especially to members of the government, one of the phases of the legal aspect of this question. I may say that opinions were obtained with regard to the contract and the Bill from some of the ablest lawyers in Canada, and I would like to read their opinion, as it is very short:
The transaction intended and provided for by the two documents of the 15th of January and 11th of February, 1901, would in substance seem to be as follows :-
The lessors in the first instrument are four railway companies in Manitoba, one at least being a Dominion corporation, and all the roads owned by them having been declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and all, we understand, being now under lease to and operated by a foreign corporation, the Northern Pacific Railway, which is a party to the agreement. These roads are all leased by this indenture to the province of Manitoba for 999 years at an annual rental commencing at $210,000 and amounting to 5300,000 after the first 30 years.
The government is to receive possession on the 1st of April next, and thenceforth to operate them and exercise all the powers and franchises of the lessors, paying the rent for them to the Northern Pacific Railway Company.
The value of the demised premises is fixed at $7,000,000, for which the lessess are to be entitled to purchase during the term.
By the second document this lease and option or right to purchase are transferred to a railway company incorporated by the Dominion, which agrees to pay the rent and perform all the covenants entered into by the government. Bonds to the extent of $20,000 a mile on 290 miles of the company's road in Ontario are to be issued, and guaranteed by the Manitoba government, secured by mortgage, subject to the company's right to pay under the option and give a first mortgage on the demised premises to raise the $7,000,000 purchase money, but such bonds are not to be delivered until the 290 miles mentioned have been completed, which is to be by the 1st of October, 1901, such bonds to replace the bonds already issued to the extent of such last mentioned bonds.
In consideration of this guarantee of the bonds and transfer of the lease and option, the company agrees that up to 30th June, 1930, the Lieutenant Governor in Council is to fix the freight rates to and from any points in Manitoba to Port Arthur and back, and from and to all points in Manitoba, the company is not to charge more, and the passenger rates are to be reduced to 3 cents per mile. The receipts are to go-first, to pay operating expenses ; next, to the rentals ; and last, to interest ; the government to bear the deficiency, if any. All companies except the Canadian Pacific may get running powers over the lines, but any amalgamation with or control by that company is prohibited. After 1905, the company is to pay the government an amount not exceeding 2 per cent of gross earnings instead of taxes, during the currency of the guaranteed bonds.
It seems obvious that this arrangement, 90 far as it is embodied in either document, cannot be carried into effect without the sanction both of the Dominion parliament and of the provincial legislature

I would call particular attention to that point.
-and the parties aware, as we suppose, of this necessity have carefully provided in each in-

strument that such legislation, If possible, shall be procured.
Until this has been obtained we think neither document can be made effective

So, it is quite clear that, unless we put this Bill through to-night Manitoba has a chance of escape.
-and we assume that the provision for the province taking over the roads on the 1st of April must have been made in anticipation of the requisite authority being secured before that date. We regard the transaction as a whole, and no portion of it can in our view be carried out effectually and safely until the whole has been ratified by both legislatures.
This is important :
It must not be understood that we think it clear that even with such legislation the proposed transaction can in all respects be made valid.
That would coincide with the views expressed in committee by the Minister of Railways and Canals that this is liable to give rise to a great flash of authority.
On the contrary, we think the arrangement by which the province of Manitoba is to obtain power to limit rates for a fixed period on parts of a Dominion railway in Ontario is at least open to doubt, and in other details the whole transaction appears to us to suggest difficulties and questions which may be found under our constitution to render the transaction as a whole impracticable.
The point they make is that Manitoba takes power under this contract not only to fix rates in Manitoba but to fix rates in Ontario. Now the question arises should this Dominion government ratify any legislation giving Manitoba the assumed power to control rates in the province of Ontario.
Several questions have been asked by telegram, which, with our answers thereto, trans-mlitted in the same way, were as follows :-
1.	Can the Canadian Northern under existing legislation by contract transfer to province as proposed by agreement the right for Lieutenant Governor in Council to fix rates ? No.
2.	If not, can such agreement be made binding by provincial legislation alone ? No.
3.	Can provincial legislature without assistance from Dominion parliament authorize the courts to direct specific performance of agreement as to freight rates, as contemplated by section nine of contract ? If the foregoing answers are right, specific performance would not be decreed.
4.	If province parted with guaranteed bonds but failed in obtaining Dominion legislation ratifying rate agreement, would province be liable to innocent holders of bonds without having any power to fix rates ? Yes.
5.	If the Dominion parliament ratified entire contract except as to rates, and company used its best endeavour as in paragraph four to obtain legislation ratifying rates but failed, would there be any breach of covenant by company ? Might province be compelled to carry out its part of contract, receiving only as consideration the reduction in passenger rates (clause ten) and right to tax (clause sixteen) ? No.
We were subsequently asked whether this answer applied to both parts of the question, to which we replied :

maintopic: FULL TEXT OF THE ACT RATIFYING CANADIAN NORTHERN CONTRACT, AS IT PASSED THE MANITOBA LEGISLATURE, MARCH 13.
speechtext:
The answer to question 5 is as intended. We thought there would be no breach of covenant by company, and that the province could not be compelled to carry out the contract if part only ratified. Both contracts expressly provide for both Dominion and provincial legislation being obtained to ratify them, and we regarded such legislation as a condition precedent to their becoming operative.
6.	Subsection 10, section 92, British North American Act, provides provinces shall have no authority to legislate respecting Dominion railways. Can the Dominion change this, or would any change in British North America Act require consent of all provinces and Imperial parliament as well as Dominion ? No.
7.	Clause 5 provides for mortgage in form satisfactory to Lieutenant Governor in Council. Can governor insist on this mortgage in any way altering provisions of contract, or is^ his right of approval limited to a mortgage strictly in accordance with the contract, but secruing by necessary provisions the carrying out of the terms of the contract by the company ? The mortgage must conform to the contract.
That is why I want the contract laicl on the Table. Here is the opinion of eminent counsel that the mortgage must conform to the contract. So we must have the mortgage before we can put this through.
8.	Do Canadian Northern and Rainy River Railways by Clause 6 of Railway Subsidies Act surrender to Dominion government control over all rates, both local and through? Yes, but these railways were already subject to the provisions in that respect of the Dominion Railway Act.
9.	Has province itself power to take control over Minnesota Railway? No.
The province cannot take control over the Minnesota Railway, and that ought to vitiate any contract, because if we cannot control that important link of forty miles, we have not got a through line at all.
10.	Can Dominion legislation provide for control of rates by province of Minnesota Railway without American legislation? No.
11.	Would it be safe for Manitoba to take control, as proposed, without providing it should only be conditional on ratification by Dominion and American legislation as to rates? No.

maintopic: C. ROBINSON, GEO. F. SHEPLEY, A. B. AYLESWORTH, H. ALLAN NESBITT.

speechtext:
These four gentlemen are the most eminent legal authorities at least in the province of Ontario. Now, I forgot to say at the outset, in justification of these remarks, that when the Bill was introduced in the House the hon. minister without portfolio, (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), who is chairman of the Railway Committee, made this statement :
I think the Bill might well be referred to the committee, with a distinct understanding that in voting for the second reading no member is committing himself to the principle or to the subject-matter of that Bill.
So that while it merely went to the Railway Committee by consent, it was on the distinct understanding that we could dis-

cuss the merits of the Bill when it came up for the committee stage. I was going to say a word as to what led to this bargain. Public men who have taken an interest in Manitoba affairs during the last ten or fifteen years will recollect the agitation we had over the question of Manitoba railway monopoly. By a clause in the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway, that company was given a monopoly of the carrying trade of the west, and the building of railways south from the main line was prohibited. Of course there was a different interpretation placed upon that clause, and it was contended by the then government, which was Conservative, that it applied to what we now call old Manitoba. Sir John A. Macdonald made the historic remark that ' we cannot check Manitoba,' meaning no doubt that the old province of Manitoba had the right to charter railways running south from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway within the boundaries of the province. That agitation was continued for years, until the province finally came to the verge of rebellion, when we saw a large body of men armed with clubs and revolvers, sworn in as special policemen-I myself happened to constitute one of them- who went up to Fort Whyte in order to force a crossing by the Manitoba system over the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was then that the Dominion government, under the leadership of the late Sir John A. Macdonald. capitulated, and made an agreement by which this government purchased from the Canadian Pacific Railway the right to allow railways to be chartered south from the main line to connect with American railway systems. In connection with that concession the Dominion of Canada paid a vast sum of money, amounting to millions of dollars. Manitoba immediately proceeded to construct a railway of its own, the Red River Valley Railway, running from Winnipeg on the west side of the Red river and connecting with the Northern Pacific system at the boundary. Now the Dominion having contributed a vast sum of money to get that privilege, a privilege which many considered was a right, it must seem desirable that we should hesitate before we dispose of this competing railway system that we introduced into that country. We introduced it at a cost of some $700,000 or $800,000, the road only cost some $3,500,000. and I rend you a statement from one of the wealthiest men in Manitoba who offered to put up $250,000 to duplicate this 350 miles of railway which has cost this country a vast sum of money, and which we are now purchasing from the Northern Pacific for $7,000.000. That being a most improvident bargain, it seems to me we ought to hesitate before we consummate it. Manitoba did not get the relief which she expected under these circumstances, there was still an agitation for amelioration of railway transportation. That agitation led to the
adoption by the Hon. Hugh John Macdonald, in the recent appeal to the country of the policy of government ownership of railroads. Upon that platform Mr. Macdonald was returned by a considerable majority. Notwithstanding that out of a legislature of forty members, Mr. Greeuway held thirty-three when they went to the country. On the policy of government ownership of railways, Mr. Greenway was wiped out and Mr. Macdonald came back with a majority pledged to carry out a policy of government ownership of railroads. Now, we hear statements made from time to time that we are getting government ownership of x'ailroads under this bargain. I think I have presented facts and figures to the House to-night which must convince all hon. members that we are not getting government ownership of railroads. It is quite true that Manitoba is leasing these railroads from the Northern Pacific, but she immediately turns round and releases them to the Canadian Northern railroad. If the Canadian Northeni is able to make these roads pay, then the Canadian Northern will pay rent to the Manitoba government: but if the Canadian Northern is not able to make these railroads pay it will pay no rent. Here let me remind the House that in the year 1900 a statement was presented, and it'is now a sworn document in the archives of this parliament, that this Northern Pacific lost $180,000 on its Manitoba lines, in operating expenses during the year 1900.
Then, I ask the House how on earth, if it loses $180,000 a year on working expenses, to say nothing of interest on bonds, will it be able to pay the rental which Manitoba will require from the company ? It cannot possibly do it. It is bound to lose money. If it loses money the company does not suffer, but the province of Manitoba has to make up the deficit, whatever it may be. Is that government ownership of railways ? No wonder the president of the labour party in the city of Winnipeg should say that instead of this being government ownership of railways it is government ownership of railway debts. These facts which I have laid before the House make the argument that it is not government ownership of railways, that is being carried out. Mr. Hugh John Macdonald, as you all know, after remaining premier of that province for a short time, resigned to contest a seat for this parliament, and being defeated, he was out of the premiership. Another premier was brought into power and another policy adopted, so that it cannot be said that the province of Manitoba pronounced, in the recent elections, in favour of the-policy adopted by the Roblin government. Nor can it be said, in view of the fact that this is a new deal, in view of the fact that this is something the people never heard of before, that if the legislature or government of Manitoba had understood its real effect they would

ever have thought for a minute of entering into a contract of this nature. In fact, in my opinion, while the people of the west are, I believe, three or four to one, in favour of the government ownership of railways, if you ratify this deal you will put the government ownership of railways beyond the pale of possibility for a great many years to come, if not in perpetuity, and that is why I say that this agreement should not be perpetrated. Let me say that any man who has read the newspapers impartially and who has followed the trend of public opinion in that country, must be convinced that public opinion is against it. Take such papers as the Montreal Gazette and others that I might mention. Even Conservative papers regard the deal with great aversion. The Montreal Gazette has continued to warn parliament that it would be a great injury to the people of Manitoba if this deal were ratified. Now, I would like to refer, in conclusion, to the point I made earlier in the remarks which I have addressed to the House, and it is that we cannot divest ourselves of responsibility in this matter. Mr. Lash, the eminent counsel who appeared for the railway company before the committee, made it perfectly clear that the legislation that we are asked for is creative legislation. It is creative legislation; it is not merely the ratification of an arrangement which has been arrived at by the province of Manitoba and the railway company. No matter how we may view this matter, we must understand one and all that we are responsible for this deal. I reiterate what I said so earnestly in my opening remarks, that the responsibility rests upon us. and that point has been made so clearly that I do not think there is any possibility of avoiding conviction upon it. We must take all the responsibility, if we force through this legislation creating a condition of affairs in Manitoba that is bound in the course of years, as the hou. Minister of Railways and Canals has said, to lead to a serious clash between the government of Manitoba and the government of the Dominion. Does the parliament of Canada desire that a serious clash should occur between these two parliaments ? Has parliament not had sufficient trouble already with Manitoba affairs to at least be very careful as to what course it may take to create trouble at the present time ? I plead to-night not to crush the deal altogether-I do not ask this House to wipe it off the slate-but to stay its hand, even if it be for a few weeks, and allow Manitoba to say, what, under the changed condition of affairs, it desires to have done. I have laid the facts before the House to show what the legislature of Manitoba thought it was acquiring when it made this deal. I have read from the words of the premier, from the mouth of the Attorney General, from the editorial utterances of their organ, and from other sources, extracts which must convince any reason-Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
able man that Manitoba understood, and understood clearly and distinctly, that it was obtaining absolute power to control rates in that province. I have shown from the record that Manitoba distinctly and clearly believed that if that contract were ratified the province for all time to come should have within its own hands the absolute power to control rates. I think it has. been clearly demonstrated that Manitoba gets nothing of the kind. I think if Manitoba at the present time understood that it was not going to receive this great boon the members of the legislature would not have hesitated one moment to repudiate the deal and in the name of the people of Manitoba and in the name of the legislature of Manitoba, I plead with this parliament to-night, and ask it that it shall allow Manitoba to say for itself what it desires under the changed condition of things. On the head of parliament, and on the head of the government, be it if it ratifies that deal without seeing that the mortgage is placed on the Table, because, as I read the contract, the contract and mortgage and the indenture go hand in hand, they must be read together, rind we have a right to know what the conditions in that mortgage are going to be. I ask that we shall stay our hand. Why should we rush through a matter like this, involving a liability of over $17,000,000 ? Is there any occasion for any great rush ? Surely, it is a reasonable demand that we should allow Manitoba to decide this matter for herself under the altered conditions, and I sincerely hope that the request that I prefer to-night that our hand shall be stayed and that at least the mortgage shall be laid on the Table of the House, shall be conceded.

maintopic: C. ROBINSON, GEO. F. SHEPLEY, A. B. AYLESWORTH, H. ALLAN NESBITT.
speechtext:
I did not at first wish to take any part in the debate, because I was willing to consider that this was very largely a domestic question, concerning the province of Manitoba. But, those who have opposed the deal have seen fit to assert that it is not a domestic question and have insisted that the members of this House, irrespective of the part of the country they represent, should judge the deal upon its merits. There may be something to be said on behalf of that argument. I have taken the advice given, I have even given some little attention to the deal, and I take the opportunity of discussing it, to some extent, according to my poor ability, upon its merits, and at the same time discussing some of the arguments that have linen made against it.
I would like to point out to the House that both in the Railway Committee and here, we have this contract denounced, in what certainly must be called unmeasured terms, and we have been instructed that the House is responsible for it in all its iniquity. But we are not asked to kill the bargain by our votes. If the bargain is half
4493 MAY 6, 1901 4494	
as bad as it is said to be, and if we are re sponsible for that badness, we have only one duty in the matter and that is to cast a unanimous vote against such an iniquitous transaction. I say that when Those who are opposed to the deal see fit to use such extreme language in denouncing it and then are afraid to follow up that language by the action for which it calls ; it argues insincerity on their part or lack of knowledge or both. The question, it seems to me, hinges on this : Have the railway rates in Manitoba been too high in the past or have they not V If the railway rates paid by the province of Manitoba in past years have been too high, then 1 claim that it may be fairly argued that this bargain is a good bargain. If the railway rates in Manitoba have not been too high in the past, then I am bound to admit that this bargain is a very bad bargain, is deserving of all that has been said against it, and I think this House will be doing less than its duty if it does not vote to destroy it. How are we going to arrive at a conclusion on this subject ? How are we going to make up our minds as to whether the railways rates in the province of Manitoba in past years have been too high or have not been too high ? What member of this House is sufficiently expert in railway matters to give an answer to this question ? I do not pretend to be, but I will bring as evidence a gentleman who I think will be admitted to have a more intimate knowledge of all railroad questions than any other in this Dominion, and a man who certainly places the interest of the railway company with which he is connected over and above -and far over and above-the interest of any province in this Dominion, or the interest of this Dominion as a whole. This is an authority which will surely be accepted as to whether the railway rates in the province of Manitoba are capable of being reduced or not, and still leave profitable earnings to the railway companies operating in that province : When the bargain between the Roblin government and the Canadian Northern Railway was announced, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway submitted to the Roblin government a rival or competitive offer, which was not accepted and which was thereafter published in the newspapers and became common property. This offer as submitted involved a reduction of railway rates and it involved the payment of considerable sums of money, and the sole and only condition of the payment of this money and of the reduction in these rates was. that the bargain with the Canadian Northern Railway should be declared off. Now I say, that if it is worth so much money to the Canadian Pacific Railway to keep out the competition of the Canadian Northern Railway, it is worth just that much anyway to the people of Manitoba to get the competition of the Canadian Northern Railway. What was the offer of the	Canadian Pacific Railway Company ? The offer was this : We will give you a reduction of 4 cents per hundred pounds upon grain shipped to Lake Superior ; we will give you a reduction of 50 cents per ton on coal brought into the country from Lake Superior ; we will give you a reduction of $2.40 a ton on salt brought into the country ; we will reduce the local rates throughout the province of Manitoba 15 per cent ; we will take over the Northern Pacific lines which you have leased at the price which [DOT] you have paid for them, and we will give you an additional cash bonus of $10,000 a year for each of the first ten years, a cash bonus of $20,000 a year for each of the succeeding ten years, and a cash bonus of $25,000 for each year of the third term of ten years. In addition we will pay the salary of a railway expert at $5,000 per annum, who shall judge as between the province and ourselves in these matters, and we will build certain specified lines of railways without bonus. Now, I have gone to the trouble of compiling a statement of what these payments in cash and these reductions in rates actually meant to the people of the province of Manitoba. One cent reduction per 100 lbs. of grain is $6,000 on each million bushels. Let us see how many million bushels the province has for export each year so that we may understand what this reduction is. According to the Manitoba crop returns, the crop of Manitoba was estimated in the year 1900 at 23,000,000 bushels, and that was a very poor crop. In 1899 the yield was 54 million bushels ; in 1898, 47 million bushels ; in 1897, 31 million bushels ; in 1896, 29 million bushels, and in 1895, 59 million bushels. It is therefore reasonable to suppose that the average yearly export of grain from Manitoba, according to the present acreage under cultivation, is no less than 25 million bushels, and a reduction of 4 cents per 100 pounds on 25 million bushels is a reduction of $600,000 a year to the people of Manitoba. I estimate the importation of salt at 4,000 tons per year, and a reduction of $2.40 a ton would be a gain to the province of $10,000 a year on the article of salt. On coal I estimate an increase of 40,000 tons, a reduction of 50 cents a ton. which makes $20,000. I take the bonuses that were agreed to be paid on account of the Northern Pacific rentals ana divide them by the term of thirty years, for which this estimate runs, and it means that the Canadian Pacific Railway was willing to pay to the province of Manitoba, over and above the rental agreed to be paid by that province, a matter of $18,333 a year in cash, for the advantage of using the Northern Pacific line. They were to pay a salary of $5,000 a year. And estimating the number of miles of rail-wav branches which they agreed to build without bonus, and estimating the Dominion and provincial bonuses to which those lines 1 would be entitled, I find that their contribu-
[DOT]1495	COMMONS	4496
tions direct to tlie province on that account, or which they would give up in connection with the building of those branches, would amount to $8,266 in cash per year for the thirty years. The offer of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to the province of Manitoba, according to the estimate which I have given-and I claim that it is within the mark-meant $761,000 a year in cold cash to the people of that province. Then, I say if it was worth $761,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway to retain a monopoly of the traffic of the province of Manitoba, it is worth $761,000 to the people of Manitoba to get the commutation they desire. I say further, if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company can afford to reduce their grain rates 1 cents per hundred pounds, and still pay interest oil a capitalization of from $30,000 to $58,000 per mile, the Canadian Northern Railway can surely carry grain at the same rqte and pay interest on an average capitalization of less than $15,000 a mile. The Canadian Pacific Railway offer was a business offer by business men for business reasons, and the fact that the offer was made without consideration to carry grain from the province of Manitoba at 10 cents per hundred pounds instead of 14 cents, which they are getting now, is evidence that this is a higher rate than the work can be done profitably for ; and if the Canadian Pacific Railway can do it for that, so can the Canadian Northern.
The changes have been rung on the possible clash of authority between the Dominion and tlie province in regard to the control of rates. There have been many reasons given why the province could not control the rates. The reasons were different oil every occasion, and the last reason is no better than the first. The last reason why the province cannot control the rates is because if it did and secured low rates within the province, shippers outside the province would be entitled to the relief which the Railway Committee of the Privy Council could afford. Ret me deal, in the first place, with the understanding had by the people of Manitoba in regard to this control of rates. It was stated specifically before the Railway Committee, and it has been stated specifically here to-night, that the people of Manitoba had been deceived in this matter-that they thought they were getting a control of rates which they did not get. The word used in the Railway Committee was. that the province had been ' gold-bricked.' Let me read from the speech of the Attorney General of the province, on the second reading of the Bill in the Manitoba legislature. If there is one member of the government who is more entitled than another to state what the law is. it is the Attorney General : and if there is one occasion more than another upon which his statement is authoritative, it is on the second reading of a Bill. If the people of Manitoba do not know the law to be as it is, then the Mr. OLIVER.
people of Manitoba have not paid attention to the statements made by their authorized legal authority. I will not trouble you by reading the whole of his statement on this subject; one or two sentences will do. Dealing with this very question of discriminatory rates, he says :
The sections that deal with this matter state that there shall be no discrimination, no special rates, and no secret special rates; and there are other restrictions.
He is telling the legislature in these words what are the provisions of the Railway Act on the very point to which'so much attention has been drawn. He says :
Now, if the contract we propose to make were a discriminatory contract, it would be had under the Railway Act; but we are making a contract which is just and equitable, and applies equally to every person in Manitoba.
He points out to the legislature that there is no ground for the exercise of the authority of the Railway Company of the Privy Council in regard to the rates which are fixed under this bargain with the railway company, because they are not discriminatory. Therefore, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, while it might have the power certainly has not the right to interfere with these rates ; and every word that has been uttered as to the absolute right of the province to fix rates in that regard, is absolutely true. But, the contention was raised in the Railway Committee, and it has been raised again here, that it is not a case of discrimination between individuals within the province, but a discrimination between individuals within the province and individuals outside the province. That is to say, when the people of the province of Manitoba fix the rates upon their produce at a certain low figure, the people outside the province, who have paid nothing towards this bargain, will claim to be entitled to have their freight carried at the same figure, and will be entitled to invoke the authority of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to compel the railway company to raise its rate against the people of Manitoba. That argument is based on a supposition which is so utterly fallacious that I am astonished at any person setting it up as an argument. It is based on the supposition that the Railway Committee of the Privy Council does, as a matter of fact, to-day prevent discrimination in railway rates between localities. It is because of the discriminations in railway rates which exist to-day against the people of the province of Manitoba and other districts of the west, which have existed for years, which have not been prevented and which never will be prevented by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, that the people of Manitoba have gone into this bargain for the purpose of getting rates equal to those given to people in other parts of this country, and to people in similar circumstances in the neighbouring country. If

It is a fact, and it is-it was stated by tlie lion, member for Saskatchewan (.Mr. Davis) here some days ago-that it costs S$ cents a bushel to carry grain at the present time from Winnipeg to Lake Superior, less than 450 miles, while grain is carried from the city of Chicago to the city of Montreal, a distance of nearly 1,000 miles, nearly 400 of which is by rail, for 4i cents per bushel- If that state of affairs exists, as it undoubtedly does, why does not the Railway Committee of the Privy Council remove it ? Because it considers that the conditions are such that there is no discrimination within the meaning of the Act. In other words, different conditions prevailing in different localities justify a difference in rates. That being the case, the House will agree tluu if there is any reason that will permit a discrimination in rates betweeen one locality and another, that reason exists in favour of the locality which has paid its good money as the price for lower rates, as compared with another which has not paid. The people of Manitoba, having pledged their credit or paid their money for the express purpose of securing lower rates, are entitled to those lower rates, and the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has no right to prevent their getting the benefit of those rates so long as that committee permits discrimination arising from different conditions throughout this country.
The idea has been put forward that the people of the North-west hope to share in the benefits of these reduced rates without paying anything. Speaking for a section of the North-west, I beg to say that no idea could be further from their minds. We understand thoroughly well that when the people of Manitoba pay their money to get a certain reduction in rates, they are entitled to that reduction, and that we who do not pay are not entitled to it. But what we do think is this, that Manitoba, having taken certain action, which, we believe, will result beneficially, has set an example to other parts of tlie country. I admit that we in the North-west have an interest in this Canadian Northern Railway. We are interested in the carrying out of this bargain, because we know that the only chance the Northwest Territories have of getting railway competition and adequate railway development is through the extension of this Canadian Northern system. Many years ago we hoped that the Manitoba North-western would give us railway development and competition, but that road to-day belongs to the Canadian Pacific Railway and is simply another link in the chain of monopoly. The North-west Central was proposed many years ago to give the North-west Territories railway accommodation and development, but that road has become another link in the chain of monopoly and furnishes no opposition. Our only chance, therefore, lies in the continuation of the Canadian Northern scheme. Therefore, we wish well to
that scheme, but that is altogether different from expecting to share in the advantage of a reduction of rates for which we are not paying anything. We do not ask for any benefits to the securing of which we do not contribute. And in this matter of discrimination, it is the Territories which will suffer, if there be any suffering. It is not the eastern provinces which will suffer. How many members present were in the Railway Committee when the . able argument was made that if the farmers of Manitoba receive certain reduced rates on their grain, the farmers of Ontario living along that line of railway, would claim a right to a similar reduction. But how many bushels of grain are raised in Ontario, or will ever be raised, along the line of that proposed railway, for export ? I venture to say that for every bushel of grain raised in the province of Ontario along the line of the Rainy River Railway, between Lake Superior and Lake of the Woods, there will be 10,000 raised in the North-west Territories. That shows the proportion of interest of two different sections of the country in this matter. If there is any section to be injured by discrimination in rates, it is the North-west Territories, but let not the House understand that the Territories consider that to give Manitoba the advantage of a reduction in rates, for which she has paid, is discrimination calling for the interference of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council.
Another point in' regard to which a very strong appeal was made to this House is in regard to the mortgage to be given in connection with this bargain. That mortgage should be laid on the Table so that the House could see really what it is. Who is going to sign that mortgage ? Who is giving the consideration for it ? Is it this parliament or government ? No, it is the government of Manitoba, and does anybody suppose that it is competent for this House to say what sort of mortgage the government of Manitoba will accept ? Surely such a proposition is not made seriously.
Surely no one can seriously propose that we should make a football of this matter and refer it back again to the people of Manitoba for further consideration. The question is certainly an important one, but it is to deal with just such questions that parliaments are elected and governments constituted. The legislature of Manitoba and this parliament were elected to deal with just such questions, and I for one hope that this parliament is not going to be so childish as to say that because a certain question is an important one. we will not consider it. but refer it back to the province, and then have the province refer it back to us. so that nothing will be done. We are here to decide these questions upon our responsibility, and if we cannot decide them, we are not fit for the position we hold.

Many arguments have been made to throw discredit upon this arrangement, and no doubt many others will be made. But, probably the poorest argument that has been put forward is that the conditions have been changed since the Bill came before this House, that is to say, that the people of Manitoba, through their legislature, voted for one thing, and that we are ratifying another. This contention is made because certain amendments have been placed in the Bill by the Railway Committee. I think X heard my hon. friend from Lisgar appeal to the House and implore the House not to commit such a breach of faith with the people of Manitoba as to pass this Act with these amendments, when the people of Manitoba were not cognizant of such conditions when the Act was passed. I am sorry my hon. friend is not in the House at the moment. I was going to recall to his memory how, a few weeks ago, he and I put up a somewhat unequal fight in this House to express more clearly, as we thought, or to explain, a statute which had been passed by parliament many years ago. And he and X argued, and I am sure we argued honestly if not ably, that it was quite within the right, as it was the duty of parliament under the circumstances, to give proper interpretation of that Act. I was astonished to find that on this occasion when an Act has not been passed, when certainly it cannot be contended that any material alteration has been made in the bargain as passed by the Manitoba legislature, that we are accused of a breach of faith and of misleading and gold-bricking the people of Manitoba, if we make what we consider necessary and desirable amendments. If these amendments that have been made or suggested, do as a matter of fact, change in any degree the tenor, or substance, or purport. of that Act, then, they should not be made. But, when, as a matter of fact, they set forth the law as it was, as it is, and as it is going to be. simply for the information of all and sundry who may or may not be interested, so that there shall be no question hs to what is meant and what is understood-so long as that is the purport and tenor of these amendments, I say that there is no ground of complaint as to their being introduced and no ground of complaint that the people of Manitoba have been deceived, and no reason for referring this Bill back to the local legislature of the province again.
The provincial legislature of Manitoba has dealt with this bargain. It has been said that the provincial legislature dealt hurriedly, that it dealt ignorantly with this contract, but that is a matter which the people of Manitoba can settle with their legislature and with their provincial government. I think it comes with rather ill grace from representatives of that province to insinuate that the local legislature and provincial government did not understand their duty and did not understand what they were doing Mr. OLIVER.
when dealing with this very important question. Is it because they are merely members of a local legislature that they are supposed not to know what they are doing, or that they are not equal to their responsibilities ? Surely, in this House we cannot hold such an argument, with so many members of our government and of this House who have served a long apprenticeship as members of the various local legislatures, and who were probably as competent men in their local legislatures or leading provincial governments as they are to-day in this House.
The arguments that have been made against the details of the Bill are arguments which should properly be addressed to the legislature of Manitoba, but I submit that they are not proper for the consideration of this House. This House, in the nature of things, cannot be aware of all the details of fact and circumstances necessary to give an intelligent judgment on these matters of detail. But, on the larger question, I am prepared to say that, if this House believes the bargain to be an improper one, if it believe it to be an immoral and ruinous bargain, it would be the duty of the House to refuse to sanction it. But that has not been shown. The very wildness of the assertions that have been made have been belied by the attitude of those who made them. So long as it has not been clearly proven that there is something outrageous or destructive in this bargain, so long as it only stands before us as a simple ratification of a contract made between a railway company and the province of Manitoba, so long, I claim we are entitled to give our consent to that bargain, our responsibility ending there. Suppose that two railway companies came here and asked for legislation with regard to their amalgamation. We might fairly take the ground for public reasons that they should not be allowed to amalgamate. But what would be thought of the House refusing to ratify such a bargain because one of the parties had not made as good a bargain as it ought, or did not understand what kind of bargain it was making. That is the argument that has been addressed to us here. We are bound to suppose that the legislature of Manitoba understood their responsibilities, and understood what they were doing when they passed upon this bargain. It is our duty to pass on our part of the bargain on our responsibility, and knowing what we are doing.
As to whether the legislature of Manitoba had a mandate on this question from the people. It has been said that the present government of Manitoba appealed to the people on the policy of government ownership of railways. I do not represent a constituency in Manitoba, but let me suggest what appeared to me to be the policy upon which that party appealed to the province. It was a policy of reduced rates on

railways. Wliat difference does it make to the people of Manitoba whether a fad under this name or a fad under that name is carried out ? What they want is a reduction of rates. You can call it by any name you please, but it was on that policy the government was elected, as I understand. What farmer or business man in Manitoba would refuse to accept a reduction in rates Which would be a benefit to him and would improve his business, on the ground that it did not come under this form or under that ? I say that the policy endorsed by the people of Manitoba was the policy of grappling with the railway question looking to a reduction of the rates. I am not here to say that this bargain is an ideal one. It is a great question. We cannot tell how it will work out until it has been worked out. But I say this-that the government of Manitoba was carrying out the mandate it had received from the people of Manitoba in the late election when it undertook this bargain.
For these reasons I support this Bill ; not because we have not responsibility with regard to it, not because I do not care whether it is a good bargain or not, but because we have responsibilities with regard to it. and because, to my mind, at any rate, it is a legitimate attempt at bringing about a better condition of affairs in regard to railway rates and the railway question generally in the western country, at grappling with the greatest and most pressing question in that country.

As this is a very broad subject which involves much more than a local question, and as several members of the House are absent, I would like the government to consent to an adjournment of the debate.

I would not like to adjourn before we reach the usual hour of adjournment.
before parliament for a long time, and perhaps during its existence. I must say that I have been much surprised to see the disposition, first of the committee and then of the House, to dispose so lightly of a matter which is characterized in such a wray by the Minister of Railways and Canals, when so many questions, not only affecting the province of Manitoba but all the provinces of Canada, are involved. It is not my intention to treat this motion from a legal point of view ; but there are some questions of great importance to be considered before we pass this new legislation which, we may say, is unprecedented in the annals of this country. Much argument has been advanced before the committee as to the power of the Federal government to divest itself of authority in favour of provincial governments in respect to legislation on railway matters. Of course, not being a legal man, I do not propose to say how far, by this Bill as it originated in the House of Assembly of Manitoba, it was proposed that the Federal government should divest itself of the power it possesses. In my opinion I think the government of Canada has no power to divest itself of any authority in railway matters, or in any other matters over which it is given jurisdiction by the British North America Act; any more than a provincial government can divest itself of power in favour of the Federal government over matters concerning which exclusive jurisdiction is given to the provinces by the same Act. Therefore, I do not propose to inquire whether this Bill is an abandonment by the Federal government in favour of Manitoba of its powers over the proposed railways dealt with by this Bill. I will say only that I think every member of this House who gives any consideration to this question will admit that the Bill proposes to give to a provincial legislature powers in railway matters which no provincial legislature has so far enjoyed under our constitution. Therefore, I say that, although there may be no violation of the letter of the law. a point which I leave to the legal authorities, the spirit of the constitution is violated by the introduction of this Bill.
Now it is said that the province of Manitoba is the only party interested in this matter, and, therefore, we have no right to discuss the merits of this Bill, that we incur no responsibility in voting for or against it. Well. I think that is a preposterous idea. Knowing that this Bill will be decided by a vote in this parliament, and therefore that the agreement will be concluded or annulled by our decision, I do not see how any one can say that we incur no responsibility. I think we incur as much responsibility in voting on this Bill as a juror does when he pronounces for or against the acquittal of an accused person. Therefore.
