speechtext:
Then I will just deal with a certain portion of the question which I think has been raised more especially by the arguments that have been advanced by the hon. member for Lisgar. I can agree with very little that has been said by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) upon this matter. First of all, I cannot agree that this is only a legal question. I agree entirely with the opinion of the Minister of Railways and Canals who told us in committee, where this Bill was discussed during several sittings, that this was the most important railway question that had come

of lowering tlie rates and therefore the people of Manitoba would be the gainers. The point that was admitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals to be the probable cause of friction between the Federal government and the provincial government w.'i s not raised in the province of Manitoba, and it was discarded by the Toronto Globe. That point is, that the Manitoba government having assumed the control of these rates for the benefit of the people of that province, they might in disregard of the interests of Ontario and Quebec or the interests of the transcontinental railway, adopt discriminating rates which would cause the whole trade coming from the west to pass over United States railways. In that event, the position of the Federal government would be either to leave as a dead letter that power of interference which is vested in it by the British North America Act (and which is repeated in the amendment suggested by the Minister of Railways and Canals) or, to interfere. And would the Federal government interfere in the way of lowering the rates in Manitoba? No. The only possible remedy would be to raise the rates in Manitoba and therefore force the Manitoba people to send their produce by Canadian railways. If the government of Manitoba have the right to ask us to give them the power to establish low railway rates for the people of Manitoba, then the people of Quebec, Ontario and the maritime provinces who have contributed towards the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway have a right to say that the government of the little province of Manitoba shall not be permitted to divest the wrhole trade of the North-west through American channels. I would hail with pleasure Canadian competition against the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am no slave of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I owe nothing to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I say, not as the representative of one province, but as a representative of the Canadian people in this Federal parliament, that we have no right to place ourselves in the position of depriving one province of the advantages we have given it, or else, allowing that province to discriminate against the rest of Canada in favour of American transportation lines. We are expending millions on our harbours, canals and railways, are we now for the sake of provincial autonomy, which is not at stake, to give to a little province, where the spirit of discrimination against the rest of the country has been developed for years; are we going to give to that province power to take the whole of the Northwest trade for which we in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces have expended over $100,000,000 of tlfe money of the people. and allow them to hand that trade over to the American railways ? We know that the people of Manitoba have no special antipathy against such a policy. We know Mr. BOURASSA.
that when the Greeuway government was in power the question was raised of the provincial government favouring the opening of a railway to Duluth. That question was discussed in the press of Canada and it was discussed in) La Patrie, just as this legislation has been discussed in La Patrie.
I have quoted the Toronto Globe to show that one of the leading organs of the government presented the question in the way that the government of Manitoba presented it; rather favourable.
The Globe had to admit that it was a very dangerous bargain, a bargain which might involve the ruin of the province, yet it said the people of Manitoba had been looking so long for the complete control of their rates, that it was no wonder they paid a high price for it. But if it had been said at that time that the Minister of Railways and Canals should come and ask the Federal government to amend that legislation, not by giving up the jurisdiction which this government has under the British North America Act, and which cannot be taken away from it ; but by asserting in that very Bill that the control of rates by the Manitoba government would be for all time to come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, I say the Toronto Globe would not have assented to that legislation. Especially, I reassert, those men, either in the legislature or outside of the legislature of Manitoba, who have gone the length of approving this legislation only on the understanding that it would be surrounded by certain conditions, would never have consented to it had they known that the Federal government proposed to deprive the government of Manitoba of the power of altering the conditions of the agreement.
La Patrie, which is one of the organs of the government, also discussed that question, and its language was much stronger than that of the Toronto Globe. On the 22nd of February last, just a week after ' Mr. Roblin had announced his policy, La Patrie come out with an editorial, which I will read, translating it from the French into English. The title itself shows the spirit of the article :

The arrangements made by the government of Manitoba with Messrs. Mann & Mackenzie deserve much more than a passing notice. It is in fact one of the most audacious deeds which our country has witnessed so far. Here is a little province, hardly capable of paying its ordinary. expenditure, which takes the responsibility of obligations involving a dozen of millions of dollars. We do not know what has been the attitude of the Lieutenant Governor, but we know what it should have been, and what it should be. Mr. Roblin should be forced to dissolve the legislature, and to ask the opinion of the electorate on this bargain, this scandalous bargain; for it is useless and even dangerous not to call things by their" names. There is evidently in this operation an enor-

mous scandal. The powerful capitalists, Messrs. Hill,, Morgan, &c., who were preparing to invade British Columbia, have their hands in this astonishing transaction which we are now witnessing. The public protest sent by a certain number of business men in Manitoba, which will be found in our columns, states nothing but the truth; but it does not state the whole truth, because the whole truth is not known. The province of Manitoba is incapable of bearing the burden which an incapable or corrupt government has just placed upon its shoulders. What will happen ? To-morrow or sometimes in the future they will come back to the federal exchequer, and ask us, the older provinces, to pay the damage. We see clearly, very clearly, through this gigantic abomination.
A piece of legislation which has been so termed by one of the organs of the government should attract the attention of the members of the government, now that we have to deal with the transaction which two months ago was so clearly seen through. With regard to the question of provincial rights, on the 18th of March La Patrie said again :
The parliament of Canada will be called on to pronounce upon this famous operation. We may find, to-morrow, if the province of Manitoba is incapable to face these heavy obligations which it has just contracted, that the Federal government will have to pay the damages. We know how prospectuses are prepared for the European market. If the parliament of Canada ratifies the Roblin deal, the prospectus that will be thrown to the world to announce the enterprise will contain in very big letters the statement that the parliament and the government of the Dominion have been brought into the bargain. Later on, if the interest on the debentures has not been paid, the bearers of those debentures will come back to us, and we shall be forced to put our hands in our pockets. The old provinces and the Dominion would be bound to face the situation.
Now, are we to be told that we have no business with this matter ? I could quote six articles of La Patrie denouncing this bargain as one of the most scandalous public deeds since confederation, stating that the parliament of Canada would have to pronounce upon it, and that we would see that the jumping-jacks of Manitoba would jump before long. It has been repeated time and again, and it is my deep conviction, that the moment the province of Manitoba realizes the result of this legislation, we shall be called upon to come to its assistance. Fifteen years ago the cry was to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. Men like Mr. Blake and Mr. Mackenzie said yes, the Canadian) Pacific Railway should be built, but pause a little and let us see how it should be built. INto, the cry was, build the Canadian Pacific Railway as quickly as possible. What was the result ? We have been told time and again that the Canadian Pacific Railway has been built, not for the benefit of the people of the North-west, but in such a way that half the people of the North-west are clamouring for other communications. Later on, when the Northern Pacific came to the frontier of
Manitoba, who had to pay for the abolition of the monopoly which had been given to the Canadian Pacific Railway ? We had to pay for it in the neighbourhood of $7,000,000. if I am not mistaken ; and now we are called upon to empower the legislature of Manitoba to assume a debt which some place at $7,000,000, which La Patrie places at $12,000,000, and which the lion, member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) places at $17,000,000. I have not yet heard one man defend the scheme as a good financial scheme. We have been simply told that this is not our business. But every time the province of Manitoba has been in a bad fix, we have had to come to its relief ; and I say it is our business, when called on to ratify this contract, to see whether or not it is a good one, because if the contract is bad we shall have to pay the damages. Therefore I say, as one of the representatives of the older provinces, and as a member of the Federal parliament, it is my duty to enter my protest first and my vote afterwards against a bargain which nobody has the courage to defend, but which is simply concealed under the pretense of standing for provincial autonomy. Sir, when a provincial government will stand for the maintenance of its rights, there will be no man readier than I am to defend its rights ; but when a provincial government enters into a bargain which has been termed by one of the leading organs of the government as a scandalous abomination, the only argument advanced in favour of a vote for this scandalous transaction is that we have no right to prevent Manitoba from ruining herself. But I know from past experience that should Manitoba ruin herself, we will be called on for the second or third time, to advance the money to get that province out of the hole. It is, therefore, my duty, as a Federal representative, and as representing a constituency in one of the older provinces, to vote against such an infamous piece of legislation. If it could be proved that this is a good bargain, that there is no danger of the province of Manitoba coming back to us for relief, I would say, let that province have the legislation it wants ; but even with the precautions taken by the Minister of Railways and Canals, I see very little chance of our preserving our rights. It is all very well in theory to say that we reserve the right of controlling the rates and of seeing that the administration of that railway is conducted on business lines ; but the hen. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) himself has told us that when the Dominion government has had to deal with private companies, it has never exercised that right. We hear every day complaints about the Railway Committee Of the Privy Council not daring to force the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway company to adopt rates satisfactory 'to the people. I ask then if the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or the Dominion government, or parliament, do not dare to exercise their rights, when dealing

with private individuals or corporations, how can they be expected to exercise those rights when dealing with a body politic, a government responsible to a whole province, and able to raise an agitation against Federal interference ? And more especially, when dealing with the province that has been preached for the last fifteen years on the principle of non-federal interference. We all remember the agitation in that province for the building of the Northern Pacific. Although at that time the Dominion government and the Canadian Pacific Railway were linked hand in hand, yet the Dominion government had to give way to the demands of the province when threatened with a rebellion. When the passions of the people are aroused, the mere text of the law will not prevent popular sentiment making its way. Not one of those men, who stand up for this Bill, will pretend that the government of Canada, which dares not interfere with private corporations in the matter of rates, will ever dare interfere with the government of Manitoba. Once we have given Manitoba the power of controlling rates, that government will exercise it to the detriment of the other provinces ; and if the Dominion government should ln-terefere, it could only do so by breaking the very principle upon which we are asked to accept this contract.
What is the use of standing here on the principle of provincial autonomy ? Either the Minister of Railways was sincere or he was not when he put a clause in the Bill retaining to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council the right to interfere and prevent discrimination. I have no doubt he was sincere, but then what will happen ? Manitoba has forced this measure upon this government in order to get lower rates. Do hon. members believe that, in dealing with the rates, the Manitoba government will have any regard for outsiders ? No, being a political administration and not the directors of a private company, and wanting to gain votes, they will make rates favourable to the people of Manitoba, and will not have the slightest regard for the interest of the people in other sections. They cannot lower their freight rates without discriminating against other parts of the country, served by this line. It is obvious that the company, with the absurd powers left to it, will endeavour to get back on that part of their line outside of Manitoba what they lose in Manitoba. So that the government of Canada will be placed in the position of either allowing that absurd state of things to continue, or else, by interfering, violate the very principle upon which we are asked to carry this piece of legislation.
In order to avoid a little agitation now, we are opening the door to a much stronger agitation in the future. There is a great tendency in this parliament to leave to our successors the burdens we ought to shoulder ourselves. The cry is:	' Let us have

peace, let us avoid agitation, let us satisfy the passions! of the moment! ' That appears to be the general policy ; but I venture to express the opinion that our duty is to enlighten the minds of the people and refuse to adopt any mistaken legislation. Nine-tenths of the members of this House condemn this legislation, but a great number on the other side will vote for it because they do not want to censure their friends in Manitoba, and members on this side will follow their example because they do not want to injure the chances of their friends in that province. But when (we have to deal with a question of this kind, which may involve the peace of this country, which may imperil the good relations which should exist between the Federal and the provincial government, we should put ourselves a little above party and deal with it on its merits. We are here not only to gain popularity, but to combat for what is right. We are bound to legislate not simply for the time-being and to gain votes, but to build up and promote peace in the country. Every day we are called on to deal with legislation for the purpose of developing the transport facilities of Canada. We are the owners of a big railway, we have built our own canals, we are deepening our channels, we are constituting ourselves a railway company and a navigation company and canal owners, and now we are legislating to take away from our railways and canals our transport facilities and transfer them to the American canals and railways. We are voting millions to secure the output of grain through Canadian ports, not only from our own Northwest, but from the American North-west as well. In the discussion on the relative merits of two Canadian ports, there was not one voice raised against the policy of having Canadian transportation at least done on Canadian soil. At least Canadian transportation should be done upon Canadian soil, and we should take from American transportation as much as we can. And now, after forty years of that policy, after the efforts of every parliament have been engaged in that way, we are opening the door to the destruction of all that work in order to satisfy a temporary agitation. Sir, it is not said, and I do not ask for my part, that this parliament should reject this legislation altogether. I do not say that the principle of provincial ownership of railways should never be sanctioned; but I do say that until we have reached the point where the Canadian government can control railways under its own authority, the least we can do is not to impair our future power in that way, and not to give the provincial governments powers which have not been contemplated by the makers of our confederation and for which they have not the proper machinery; but in regard to which they are bound to come to us to help them, and in so doing

put us In tlie position where we are at once the legislative power giving them the rights which they do not possess, and also the executive power ruling over another executive power which is entirely outside of us and beyond our jurisdiction in every other matter. We are making this a most absurd position legally, financially, and politically, and when we try to avoid our responsibility by saying that the people of Manitoba want it, we are simply taking a side issue in order to avoid facing the question itself. Suppose that to-morrow the legislature of the province of Quebec were to adopt a Bill to authorize the Superior Court judge in Hull to take charge of the administration of justice in the county of Carleton and were to ask us to ratify it- they would represent that it was for the benefit of the people of Quebec, and that this was a matter under provincial authority. Under a particular provision of our constitution the Dominion government has the power to appoint the judges, while the provincial authority has the right to arrange the judicial districts of the province. Suppose the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario were to enter into such a bargain, we would never sanction it. because it would be an absurd thing to bring two provinces together in this way which are so different in their constitution. It is no more absurd to give one province legal jurisdiction in the territory of another than to give a provincial government a right to control railway rates outside of its own boundaries, or even within its own boundaries injuriously affecting the interests of others. And even if it is objected that in this case we keep our control, I say that we do not keep it in effect, or that we can keep it only by breaking the only principle upon which, I think, we can base our granting of that legislation.
I cannot vote for the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg-not that I am opposed to the principle of the referendum, but because we should not on a matter of special legislation adopt that principle. I am prepared, however, to vote for the motion of the hon. member for Lisgar. In doing so, I am simply following the course to which I will not say I was inspired by the articles of La Patrie, but that came to my mind when I read those articles. We do 'not repulse the legislation or say that we will not adopt it, but we say to the people : You adopted the bargain, you adopted it for such and such a reason and because you thought it would give you such and such advantages; but it having come before us we cannot grant it as it is; we make the amendments that we think proper, and send it to you to see if you will concur in them. I say that, to my mind, the whole thing is wrong- there should be no such legislation. I would rather vote against the whole thing as I* indicated in committee. But, if we are to pass over the objections which are so 142
serious, and if we are to adopt this Bill, at least let us not adopt it after only two or three hours discussion and without knowing what are the real intentions of the people whom we want to please so far that we are ready to break the spirit of our constitution to please them. And when we are told by their representatives, and not only their representatives here but their local representatives, that they have adopted this only with such and such intentions, I do not see that we are doing very much to please them when we impose on them conditions which they did not contemplate and which they refuse to execute. Let us send back this legislation, if we cannot do better. If the government does not press the vote upon the whole of this legislation, which I think it would not be wise to do, and if there is time under the rule regarding notice, I will propose an amendment to clause 3 which has already been amended by the Railway Committee at the proposal of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. The clause that was added to by the minister provided :
Nothing in this Act or in the indenture contained in the schedules hereto, or done in pursuance of this Act or of the said indentures shall

Then there are subsections a, b and c, the last of which says :

And there at the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals were inserted the words ' any discriminating rate for the carriage of freight or passengers or to allow or make any secret or special tolls, rebates, drawbacks or concessions.' I would move, on the third reading that after the words ' discriminating rate ' the words he inserted : ' in favour of or against either (1) ,any individual or corporation, or (2) the people or shippers of or from any particular place, section, district or province.' The object is to cover the point I have just stated, that if we are called upon to legislate in favour of the province of Manitoba, we should not forget the rights of the other provinces and the rights of the large transportation companies, in case the province of Manitoba should, as seems to me very probable, to discriminate in favour of American railways. I wish to be well understood on this point. I do not mean to check competition between, for instance, the' Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific. Let these fight each other as much as they please and the people will benefit by it. But I am strongly opposed, in case it would be favourable to the people of their own province, to the provincial government sending their traffic to the south, which they could do easily, because a part of this line Is through the state of Minnesota and it has easy connections with lines in the United States. We must provide that, not only in



case of a company or individual coming to the railway company of the Privy Council, shall that committee interfere to stop discrimination ; but supposing, for example, the province of Ontario, having subsidized part of this line, were to come and tell the government of Canada : ' We have contributed to the building of these railroads because we were told by the law that they were under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal parliament. Now, if the Federal government propose to give to the Manitoba government jurisdiction over these railways, the Manitoba government may legislate in a manner antagonistic to our interests. We want to be protected against discrimination.' Of course. I do not think this government can divest itself of any of its powers in these matters. When the Minister of Railways and Canals proposed these amendments, he said he wanted the people of Manitoba to understand their position. Well, if they are given to understand that the provincial government cannot discriminate against individuals. let them he told also that they cannot discriminate against whole provinces. It only gives the conclusion of the Attorney's speech. The Attorney General begau his speech on Friday and he finished it on Monday, and it is only his Monday speech that is published in this supplement. On Friday the Attorney General said :
It is the intention of the government that the government will absolutely control the rates, and that the rates will be fixed so that no one but the Lieutenant Governor in Council will be able to disturb them.
The Attorney General preached absolute control, and that no power was entitled to interfere with these rates but the Lieutenant Governor. Andj yet the Attorney General has been quoted in this House by the hon. member for Alberta to show that he ] said that this parliament would retain the | first control. The Attorney General further , said :

The board of trade reported that the government should make provision for passenger rates. Mr. Campbell said that they had not been able to, but they would endeavour to do so. That was the meaning of the Attorney General's speech on Friday afternoon, and he finished that speech on Monday. In the supplement which has been distributed freely in Ottawa, the Monday's part of his speech has been given in a form from which I imagine the hon. member for Alberta has drawn his conclusion that the Attorney General did not say that there was absolute control within the power of the province. There is no doubt that the premier of the province all along recommended the bargain because it gave absolute control of rates to the province; and the . only thing that makes the motion that has been moved by my hon. friend from Lisgar of any effect is the question whether we have changed the Act at all, or whether we have put any construction upon it or imposed any conditions which the Manitoba legislature did not do. Our amendment to section 3 of the Bill, which is now7 before the House, stating specifically on the initiative of the Minister of Railways, that this government retains to itself all control of rates, and that there shall be no discrimination, was evidently inserted, as the Minister of Railways told us it was, because there might still be some people in Manitoba who imagined that they were claiming the control of rates. If there is any alteration in the contract, then the motion now7 before us is a good one, because we are passing some other proposition altogether, and are not doing w7hat the legislature of Manitoba asked us to do. It was a surprise to every member of the Railway Committee to find the legal counsel of the railway company making suggestions to amend the Act, and the counsel of the province of Manitoba immediately accepting those suggestions before they were made, and before he could possibly have known their import. I submit that if we cannot alter the law as it w7as passed by the legislature of Manitoba, most certainly the counsel representing the executive committee of that government cannot do so. I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to go very fully into this matter, because it was very fully dealt with by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) on the previous motion; but lam just going to quote a few7 remarks of the premier of Manitoba in which he did say many times that this bargain meant the absolute control of rates in that province. The proposed contracts were first announced on the 14th of February, by the premier at a banquet at Neepawa, and the next day the Winnipeg Telegraph, the organ of the local government, heads its editorial column with this very emphatic statement :
Splendid bargain. Control of rates has been secured to the people of Manitoba.
That is the first sentence in the editorial column.
That was the message of Premier Roblin last night, enthusiastically endorsed by every member of the cabinet. No matter how critically the contracts can be examined, no interpretation can be put upon them which will take away from the people of Manitoba the control of rates.
Now, I ask the hon. member for Alberta, or any other lion, gentleman who has contradicted the statement that these acts were put through the Manitoba legislature on the direct assurance of the premier and the Attorney General that absolute control of rates w7ould be obtained, what can be learned by this last sentence V Since this Bill has been before the Railway Committee every lawyer who has spoken, and every man who has analysed the matter, has come to the conclusion that the province of Manitoba has not control of rates, but that we must control rates and cannot divest ourselves of that power, and the Minister of Railways has himself suggested the insertion of clause 3, which is already in the Railway Act, so that there might be no doubt on that point. But there was no other consideration on the part of Manitoba , than the absolute control of rates; and if we cut that away or state that it was never there, then I claim that the amendment now proposed is the right one. The article goes on to say :
The object of government ownership, of railway commissions and of all other public methods of regulation is the control of rates, and this the government has secured in the most direct form. The rates are to be fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
The premier, in opening his speech that night, mentioned that his government had heen elected among other things on a government ownership platform, and he had said then that the only object in their wanting government ownership was to get absolute control of rates. It is said we are not far enough advanced to entrust the ownership and management of our railways to any government, and to that extent government ownership is impracticable; hut if we have not government ownership, we have absolute control of rates, and therefore we have got that wltnout the trouble we would have incurred otherwise- there is very little doubt that this was the meaning of the premier's statement at that time. His own paper the next morning contained probably the most emphatic deliverance given on that point. It absolutely settles the question whether the people of Manitoba were told that they were getting control of rates in this deal.

That means that the people of Manitoba will enjoy a privilege enjoyed by no other province in Canada.
The hon. member for Labelle argued that if we cannot give discriminatory rates to individuals, we cannot give them to a province, but we have the most explicit statement by the First Minister of Manitoba that the Lieutenant Governor in Council would have absolute control of the rates. I do not know that there could be any plainer statement. The gentlemen who initiated this bargain and put it through, informed us that the Lieutenant Governor in Council has the right to make all tariffs from that time forward until the contract is revoked-that is for thirty years. That is what they promised the people of Manitoba in return for their guarantee of $17,000,000 of bonds. I do not know whether these gentlemen had considered the Railway Act of Canada or the authority of this parliament under that Act. If they had, they would have come to the conclusion that they were evading it. If they had not, then they were simply misleading the people.
The position of the hon. member for Alberta and of those who deny that we have altered the contract which was passed through the legislature of Manitoba, was not what it was represented to be to the members of that legislature and the people of the province.
A strong point of the hon. member for Alberta was that because the Canadian Pacific Railway came along and offered to buy out this deal altogether-offered so much in reduced rates and taxes and in foregoing the asking of bonuses on lines to be constructed -practically offered Manitoba a very large sum if the Manitoba government would not enter into this deal, therefore, that offer represented what the deal was worth to the people of Manitoba, and what it would save them. I do not think that that is a proper ground to take. The Canadian Pacific Railway simply wanted to head off this deal and have an absolute monopoly. It could see that its competitors were getting stronger, that the ratification of this deal would make one of tlidm stronger, and it also saw an opportunity to buy out all opposition and was willing to pay a very good sum. But if this measure becomes law, the province of Manitoba will find that it will not gain anything like the sum offered by the Canadian Pacific Railway. It will find that if the people get lower rates they will have to pay very dearly for them. If the rates in Manitoba are reduced below the carrying price, the province will have to make up the deficit and the people of the Territories will want the same rates. You cannot discriminate on the one line of railway between different points. You cannot have higher tariff on the one side of a provincial line than on the other. And despite the statement of the hon. member for Al-Mr. PUTTEE.
berta, you will find deputations coming down from the Territories to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, demanding that the rates be equalized, and the rates will have to be equalized either by reducing them in the Territories or raising them in Manitoba. We can easily foresee a conflict between the government of Manitoba and the government of the Dominion on that very point. Unfortunately, Manitoba has the worst end of the stick, and will have no remedy but to put up the rates, and still go on paying the interest on the bonds.
There is one other point to which I draw attention. A good deal of legal opinion was obtained from the railway lawyers of the country on these deals, and, to refute some of these opinions, the organ of the local government got some opinions itself, and this one signed by Walter Barwick. His opinion on clause 8, I think, is worthy of the attention of this House in the light of our being, as we were practically told that if we refused to pass this legislation we should be vetoing the action of Manitoba. There was no such suggestion from Manitoba, and their counsel has explained that to them most satisfactorily for he says that if similar legislation to that passed by the legislature of Manitoba is passed in the Dominion parliament nothing more will be required to make the contract, including clause 8 fully efficient and to enable the transaction to be carried out. This gentleman, being the adviser of the government tells them that similar legislation must be passed by the parliament of Canada. I submit that that is entirely different from vetoing or disallowing an Act. It seems to me that the case that was made out before the Railway Committee is supported by this opinion and that the legislation of this parliament goes almost to the extent of the creative. At all events, in acting in this matter we must take the responsibility and that responsibility seems to me to involve the duty of thorough investigation into the clauses of this agreement; and, if they are not right, if there is conflict between the two authorities, if the people of Manitoba have not the Act that they expected, then we should send it back to the legislature. I am sorry that there is an intention to force the Bill through the committee stage to-night. I have been surprised to see that in the Railway Committee and in this House we have had no expression of opinion from the members of the government or from other members of the House who are certainly more familiar with railway matters than I am, or from members representing Manitoba constituencies. It seems to me that we are deluding ourselves with the idea that this is no concern of ours. But I cannot understand that the government can be without responsibility if the statement made by the Minister of Railways in the Railway Committee is to be accepted. After that statement, I cannot see how the hon. gentleman can leave the matter to go

through without a word. It is clear that it is not known what the effect of this agreement will be. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals stated that the principle included in the Bill has never been before this parliament since it was1 a parliament. It being so serious a matter, I can quite understand why he should be careful. He is in a position where he cannot allow his authority to be taken away, nor can he allow an Act to go through that will bring a clash between his authority as chairman of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council and that of the province. Of course, we know that the motion that is now submitted will not have the support that the motion should have, but I am quite willing to support it. I believe that the motion that I submitted to the House even if it would not get the support even that this one would, is the best solution to the difficulty. This is not, as the hon. member for Alberta, says, simply a matter of trying to shirk responsibility. We should not deal with this matter iu committee until we have some assurance as to what it is we are asked to pass. It lias been pointed out already this evening that the mortgage which is referred to in this Act is more than an ordinary mortgage, because the government refused to amend the Act but declared that they would cover all desirable amendments in the mortgage. In fact, if there is any virtue in this bargain, it is to be found in the mortgage which not merely becomes part of the Bill but is to govern. It is of greater importance than the Bill itself. And we have no indications as yet what its terms are to be. To that extent we are passing this Bill in the dark. I shall have much pleasure in supporting the motion of the hon. member for Lisgar.

I think this question had better be disposed of this evening or this morning rather ; it will be only a waste of time to prolong this discussion further. Every gentleman in the House has made up his mind how he will vote on this question. I am not a representative of Manitoba or of the North-west, but I have a good deal of sympathy with the people of Manitoba. They are about the centre of this Dominion, and their interests should be watched over by this Dominion government. If the people of Manitoba have made a mistake, as it has been shown that they have, and are likely to be injured by the Act of their legislature, when they come to the Dominion parliament and ask en-dorsation of what they have done. I think this Dominion parliament should be very careful what they do about it. I do not suppose, from the discussion that has taken place, that there will be very many who will vote for the hon. member for Lisgar's resolution, but I intend to vote for it. I think the resolution is a very fair one. No one will be injured by postponing this matter for at least a few months, and I think it would be wise for us to allow it to go back to the legislature of Manitoba. But to prolong this discussion, thinking we will get more members to believe as we do, will be useless. I think it will be better to have this vote taken to-night ; we would only lose more time and gain nothing by delaying a vote. I think hon. members have already said more than was necessary to say on the question. It seems to me that any man ought to be able to say in half an hour all that can be said upon it.

I do not want to offer any obstruction at this stage ; but, I must express my surprise at the announcement of the Prime Minister, that the government do not take any position as a government on this Bill. It is surprising to find that during the whole of this discussion the Minister of Railways and Canals has been absent from his seat, in view of the position he took in the committee, where he stated that this was the most important railway question that had ever come before the parliament of Canada since confederation. Now, while this discussion is going on in this House, when suggestions are made and opinions are asked, we find that the member of the government who has care of the railway legislation, who is called upon to advise parliament in relation to it, who is charged with the duty of maintaining the rights of the people in railway matters, is absent from his seat. More than that, no member of the government has given his opinion on the matter. I regret to observe that although the government say they do not take any responsibility on this question, as a matter of fact they do take responsibility for it, because they propose to force this measure through, and they resist an adjournment which is proposed in order to allow absent members to express their opinion upon it. Why is it that the government do not openly assume responsibility ? Is it because they are still of the opinion that La Patrie was, that this is the most abominable bargain that was ever entered into by any government ? If they are of that opinion, how is it that when they are asked by men who have no desire to obstruct, to define their position, to say how far they consider these amendments are in accordance with the terms made by the government of Manitoba, no answer is' vouchsafed us ? Now we find that after the government organ has denounced this bargain in eight leading articles for one month and a half, the government have no responsibility, nothing to say, no directions to give parliament. Sir, the scandalous transaction is not confined to Manitoba, but it is in this House. The matter had been kept upon the ground where it was discussed for about fifteen days. After the announcement made by the Prime Minister of Manitoba, papers of all

shades of opinion in all the provinces took up the question and discussed it on the merits, as well as on the various constitutional points ; and then the discussion grew more acute every day ; the government organs and the opposition organs took the strongest ground possible upon the question, but still the government have no policy ! Here the leaders of the two great parties are called upon to vote upon the question. We are told that there is no polities in this question, that it is only a question of business. Why, Sir, the whole thing is a question of politics, and instead of being a question of open politics, it is a question of hidden politics. It is a question of hidden interests that are not revealed. How is it that La Patrie was so outspoken a month ago, and that now we cannot get any member of the government to express an opinion upon it ? For a month and a half we have been promised revelations, we have been told by one government organ that the powerful syndicate of Hill and Morgan was at the back of this arrangement ; but now we have no information, no opinion from the government. Is it because the syndicate was so powerful as to shut our mouths ? Is it because the truth that was going to come out is now too big to be given to the people? Well, Sir, I do not think that either the leader of the government or the leader of the opposition are gaining anything by this little game. They may gain a little advantage in Manitoba for the present, but they do not gain any moral advantage before the people. The people are prepared to forgive many things in their public men, they are prepared to forgive mistakes, acts of bad policy, but they are not prepared to forgive moral cowardice, and unfortunately we see too much of that very often in this House.
Order.
I must ask the hon. member to withdraw that expression, that he has seen too much moral cowardice in this House.

All right, I will withdraw the expression with pleasure, because I always desire to obey your ruling, and to maintain the discussion on a proper footing. But, I will keep my own opinion just the same. If I am out of order in calling this moral cowardice, I will try to find another word, but my tongue is not so supple in English as in French, and so I will employ a sentence. I will say that it is strange to find the government in that position, that a great public question has come before us involving the interpretation of the constitution, involving the relations of the Federal government with the provincial government, involving the future of the transportation problem of Canada, involving the financial future of one province, involving the direct interests of the federal-for the time will come when that province will Mr. BOURASSA
be unable to fulfil its obligations, and It will come to this government for aid-yet, Sir, a question like this is treated by hon. gentlemen on both sides as of less interest than the simplest private Bill. Why, if a private Bill incorporating an ordinary railroad company were before this House, involving only a tithe of the political and financial problems which this legislation involves, we would have the opinions of half the ministers and of the leader of the opposition. How is that none of these hon. gentlemen spoke on the second reading of the Bill ? It was because they wanted to get details. Let the Bill go into committee, they said, let it be threshed out, then when we are in the possession of all the details, the House will pronounce itself.
The committee devoted three or four sittings to the consideration of the question. Strong expressions of opinion have been given by ministers of the Crown and by leaders of both parties. We have been told that this is the most important question that has been discussed for a long time and certainly the most important question that has been discussed this session. We have been told that we should deal very carefully with the matter. We have been given evidence that this legislation has been adopted by the people of Manitoba under certain conditions and that these conditions, having been found improper, we have been asked by a representative of the government to alter them. Now, when we are asking the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to complete the opinion that he gave in the Railway Committee, we see that the hon. gentleman is not in his seat. How is it that an opinion that was proper to be given in the Railway Committee where there is no ' Hansard,' where the words uttered by members are not taken down is not repeated here when parliament is called upon to pass upon this legislation and to adopt or reject the decision of the Railway Committee ? How is it that the hon. minister who said in the Railway Committee that if the committee passed this legislation it might and probably would bring about a clash between the Federal government and the provinces is absent and we cannot get an expression from the representatives of the government or from the leader of the opposition ? But, we are told that this Bill must pass to-night. We are told that no more time should be given to this legislation.
No such statement as that has been made. There was no attempt made to force it at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I think the hon. minister was not here when the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) was before the House. I got up at 11.30, and I said that I had an amendment which certainly was not an obstructive amend-

ment, which was an amendment that should be discussed which I wanted to move in committee and that if the government were ready to take the vote upon the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg we could adjourn until to-morrow or any day so that we could discuss the motion of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson), give a day to it and then take a vote in committee. Mr. Speaker, we have been told, I repeat, and I insist upon this point, that this is the most important railway question that we have dealt with for thirty' years, and we are told now that three days discussion is too long for this question. Small Bills of the merest local importance are discussed for hours. When we are in Committee of Supply members will get up and discuss for half an hour or three-quarters of an hour the price of nails, or screws, or something of that kind involving an expenditure of $10 or $15. A big discussion will take place and inflamed speeches will be made on an expenditure of that kind. Time will be given to questions of no importance whatever, but when a question, which, according to the declaration Oif a representative of the government. is the most important that we have had to deal with for years, two days discussion, or three days discussion is too much -a question which has been denounced by one of the leading organs of the government as the most scandalous that has to be dealt with. The truth was to come out, but the truth does not come out. I suppose I must refrain from using words which I would like to use, but I will say what the attitude, not only of the government but of parliament, inspires me. It reminds me of the worst phases of the Congress of the United States at a time when some railway Bills could be passed without any discussion and without any consideration, because the proper amount of lobbying work had been done. I do not say that lobbying work has been done in this matter, hut, here is a question which has been presented to the public under the darkest colours ; and the way it is treated in this House by the leaders of both parties is not of such a character as to inspire respect for parliament or respect for their representatives by the people of Canada. The people have been told for two months that their greatest interests were involved in this legislation, that the future of this country might be involved and now, when we are asking an expression of opinion from a member of the government who gave expression to the sentiments to which I have referred in the Railway Committee, he is absent. We are told that the Bill must pass and we are told that nobody assumes any responsibility. How is it that the men who stood up in the Railway Committee against the Bill, are now absent ? How is it that men who had the intention
of speaking on the second reading and who were told by another minister of the government that if they reserved their speeches for the time when the Bill was in committee or for the third reading that their letting the Bill pass its second reading without any discussion would not imply any consent on their part to the principle of the Bill, are now all gone ? Because three or four members ask for the opinion of the government they are called obstructionists. It is not my intention nor is it in my power to offer any obstruction to this Bill. I do not represent the interests of the province of Manitoba, but I represent the interests of the people of Canada, and I have a right in that capacity to ask how it is that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is not here to-night. How is it that we have no expression of opinion from the leaders of both parties ? How is it that this legislation which has been painted in such dark colours by the leading organ of the government is to be rushed through the House without argument or discussion ? I am not going to detain the House any longer, but I protest most strongly against the way this Bill has been dealt with in the House and in the committee. The truth has not come out, but, the truth will come out one of these days and perhaps some of the majority, some of those who are going to vote, although they know it is a bad bargain, though they have been told that it is a bad bargain, but who will vote because this man or that man voted for the Bill and who will shelter themselves under the lame excuse that they are respectful of provincial autonomy, even to the point of voting for legislation that they say is backed up by the capital of an American syndicate, the most powerful syndicate that the world has ever known, will discover their mistake. Let not the people of Canada remain in the dark that surrounds this huge transaction, this huge bargain which has been denounced by the government organs and by some of the opposition organs. Some of the Conservative newspapers have also denounced this bargain, the Hamilton Spectator and others. I am not going to lengthen my remarks, but, in taking my seat I repeat that as a representative of the people and as a representative of the province of Quebec I protest most strongly against the way in which this question has been dealt with in the Railway Committee and in the House of Commons.

I think this mock heroic has gone far enough. These hon. gentlemen who have spoken think they have all the intelligence and all the honesty in this House. I am able, I hope, to give an intelligent vote, but I will not sit silently here to listen to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and the hon. member for Lisgar (Sir. Richardson) claiming all the honesty of this parliament to themselves.

Mr. BOtIRASSA. I did not assume anything. I simply go to La Patrie and state that after these articles we should have the truth.

The hon. gentleman seems to be unable to form a judgment unless he can base it on something that has appeared in a newspaper. I submit that a member of this House ought to be able to form a judgment for himself. It is not the first time that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa) has found himself in a wretched position upon questions before this House. When he stands up here and tries to monopolize all the honour and all the wisdom of this House, I would suggest to him that he might perhaps add modesty to his characteristic of volubility. First of all, the question for us is : Has this parliament power to pass this legislation. I emphatically assert that there is no question of our right to do so. I suppose that members of the government, like others, think that when a very small minority is protesting, enough has been said on the question, and that the business of the House should proceed.
I suppose it was only discussed a few minutes in the Railway Committee ?
It was discussed for three days there.
For four days.

I beg pardon, for four days. These gentlemen think that because they assume all the knowledge about the question, that their statements must be taken as a matter of fact, and that they must be answered in this House. Well, after all, there are certain statements made by certain gentlemen which do not merit a reply. I do not assume that I possess all the knowledge of this House, nor do I pride myself on my intellect as the member for Labelle does, but I do humbly and modestly submit that this parliament has the power to pass this legislation. Honest men will differ upon the merits of this question, but let us differ without being vain and without being puffed up with the idea of our own superior knowledge. Let us present our arguments without assuming that every man who agrees with us is honest, and that every man who disagrees with us is dishonest. This parliament is the place for hon. gentlemen to express their views modestly and firmly, and to leave to their fellow members and to the country, to decide whether they are right or not. It may be a question for us to consider whether after all certain gentlemen in this House possess so much brain power as these gentlemen themselves think. The member for Labelle hinted that there was some power outside.
I know of no such power. I have my simple duty^ to perform as a member of parliament, and if the province of Manitoba saw fit to Mr. FRASER.
enter into this contract, I assume that the province knew just as much about it as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) or the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson). I assume that the Manitoba legislature, fresh from the people, knew exactly what was in the best interests of the people of that province.
May I ask the hon. gentle man if there has been any protest from any members of the Manitoba legislature who voted for this measure, since then, against the ratification of the contract ?

I know of no protest either from those who voted in favour of it or those who voted against it. I repeat, that I am justified in assuming that the members of the Manitoba legislature knew just las much about this question as does the member for Labelle.
Oh, no.

I may be wrong, but that is my opinion. But, Sir, beyond all this, there is a serious question. Our confederation is now in the successful process of its development. I do not want that to-day or to-morrow, certain persons who feel agrieved at provincial legislation, should be continuously appealing to this parliament to ask us to declare that the legislature did not know what it was doing. I know something of the construction of the republic to the south of us, and I know that year after year the struggle between the states and the federal authority went on until at last it had to be settled by the shedding of the blood of hundreds of thousands of her best citizens. I am not anxious that this Federal parliament should be continuously asked to decide whether a provincial legislature, acting within the purview of its rights, passed wise or unwise legislation. We have enough to do in this parliament without considering these questions. I claim no more honesty than others, but I do claim that the great majority of members in this House have no right to be subjected to such lectures as we have had from the member for Labelle to-night. I assume that Manitoba has the right to pass that legislation.
' Manitobar.'

No. * Manitoba.' I will insist on my own pronunciation as against the pronunciation of any hon. gentleman who sets his up against mine. Manitoba had a right to pass this legislation, and for my part I am willing to supplement it by legislation here. I do not see the consequences that are going to flow, as represented by the gentlemen who speak on the opposition side. I am willing that the judges and those interested shall decide, and I am willing to give them that opportunity. Surely the hon. gentleman will permit me to do that without being branded as either lacking in intelligence or patriotism, or the

ordinary honesty in which they live and move and have their being. They may combat that position by argument, but let them not assume that we must await the return of one hon. member of this House in order to get proper light on this question, in addition to what they have given. I am here to discuss questions, and to vote on them, in order that I may get home as quickly as possible. I regret that the hon. member is absent, but I do not sigh for his return ; for, having heard him express his views in the committee, I do not know that he would have added anything new to the able, fair and inexhaustible arguments the hon. gentlemen themselves have given. Now, my position on the question is this, that Manitoba has seen fit to enter into certain contracts with a company subject to the action of this parliament. That company have come here and asked us to permit them to do so. I see no difference between giving the power to the company beforehand and giving it now after we know the facts. Hon. gentlemen say that the bargain i's a bad one. I am not going to discuss that at any length. I submit that the whole question is a problematical one at most, and I am not going to assume that two or three gentlemen in this House are possessed of all the wisdom on that question. I am still going to have my opinion, that we should leave it to the parliament of Manitoba. Do hon. gentlemen think they are going to advance the position they have taken or the pledges they have given by not permitting this measure to take its proper stage this evening ? Let us do that and then let them discuss on the third reading, if they see fit, the further developments they may be permitted to make. But, I trust that in the discussion of this question we will assume that all the wisdom is not contained in one head, and that we may honestly differ on the question without it being hinted by gentlemen on the other side that we must be wrong, not only in our intellectual appreciation of the question, but in some dark way which they have not explained. I will vote for the motion because I think there is no legal disability on the part of this parliament to pass the measure, and because Manitoba is the best judge of the question. I cannot see that there is the danger before us which the hon. gentleman has pointed out.

I realize that I have not a right to speak on this question again ; but, I was going to say. in response to a statement which the hon. gentleman made, that when we took the second reading of the Bill, and referred it to the committee, it was on the distinct understanding that the House was not in any way committed to it. If we advanced it a stage now. the House would be committed to the principle of the Bill, and for that reason I would like to have the hon. member for North Norfolk here.
